(bright music) - Potential complications
after liver transplant can generally be grouped into
the following categories. Problems with the blood
vessel connections, the bile duct connection, related to medical
conditions, or medications. In addition to this, bleeding
is a common occurrence in liver transplant. It may occur during the operation or in the first few days
following the transplant and it may require a return
to the operating room to fix bleeding or remove blood clots. Liver disease itself makes people at increased risk for bleeding. One of the jobs of the
liver is to make protein that helps the blood clot. It can take the new liver a bit of time to get back to normal levels of function. Blood transfusions at
the time of transplant and in the few days after
transplant are common. You may be at more risk for
some complications than others based on your other medical problems or how ill you are at
the time of transplant. We will review the other
types of complications in more detail. Blood vessels are tubes that carry blood throughout the body. When we make connections
between your blood vessels and the blood vessels of the new liver. I like to ask people to think of it like hooking two garden hoses together. Our goal is to allow blood to flow easily through the new connection from your body into the new liver, and
then back into your body. The blood vessels may
become narrowed or kinked due to handling, the new
connection, or positioning. If we have suspicion
that the blood vessels are narrowed or kinked based on tests, we have several ways we approach this. Sometimes we use blood
thinners to keep the blood from getting clogged in the narrowed area. Sometimes, we place a straw
or stent through the narrowing in order to prop it open and allow flow. On rare occasions, we have to
return to the operating room to redo this connection. What we want to avoid, or
prevent from happening, is blood cells getting
stuck in the narrowing and leading to clogging or
clotting of the blood vessel. If the blood vessel becomes
completely clogged or clotted, it can cause the liver not to function. This happens infrequently, but may require that we
perform a new transplant. Early re-transplantation
occurs infrequently, less than 5% of the time. Reasons for early re-transplant include blood vessel complications, and also a situation termed
primary non-function. Primary non-function is a situation where in spite of the
liver looking acceptable on paper and in person, and
the operation being fine, the liver does not function appropriately for reasons that we do
not completely understand. In these situations, we do a new transplant
as soon as possible. You may get a special
status on the waiting list, placing you at the top
of the waiting list. The bile duct is a tube
that carries digestive fluid from the liver to the intestine. Complications with the
duct include leaking or narrowing of the connection. If we have suspicion that there is a narrowing of this connection, we do a procedure called an ERCP. This procedure is similar to an EGD where we use a video camera
to look into your stomach. However, in an ERCP, we look further into the
area of the intestine, which is connected to the liver. In an ERCP, the video camera
views into the intestine and we look for any narrowing in the connection to the liver. If there is narrowing, temporary straws, or tubes, like these
blue tubes shown here, are placed into the duct
to stretch the connection. In six to eight weeks,
the procedure is repeated. If the narrowing persists,
the stents are replaced. If the narrowing has resolved,
the stents are removed. In rare situations, we have to
return to the operating room to fix an area of narrowing. After liver transplantation,
you will take medications to prevent rejection for
the rest of your life. These medications help protect your body from attacking the new liver
and causing damage to it. The same cells that are weakened in order to protect the new liver are the cells that help protect
our bodies from infection and guard against
abnormal appearing cells. Because of this, these
medications increase your risk of infection and cancer. The most common cancer following liver transplant is skin cancer, so it is important that you use sun protection after transplant, and that you see a skin
doctor once a year. There are some lifestyle changes that go along with transplant
that are largely targeted at decreasing your exposure to infections. You will learn more about these during the evaluation process. Survival following transplant is very good with the one-year post-transplant survival being greater than 90%. Issues during the first
year are largely related to the complications of
surgery previously discussed, as well as infection. The five-year post-transplant
survival is 75 to 85%, and may be affected by medical problems you have unrelated to transplant. (bright music)

Welcome! The purpose of this video is to explain the
liver transplant evaluation process. Your liver transplant evaluation is a 3-step
process: Meet your transplant team,
Perform physical and laboratory testing, and the
Transplant committee meeting When you meet your transplant team, your carepartner
should also be present. Your nurse coordinator will be your contact
person throughout the evaluation. Your transplant hepatology doctor specializes
in diseases of the liver. The transplant surgeon will perform your liver
transplant surgery. The social worker will assess assistance you
may need from a financial, social, substance use, or mental health perspective. The dietician will discuss your nutritional
needs. You may also talk with a
Financial advocate pharmacist,
researcher, psychiatrist, and
Heart or anesthesia doctor While meeting with each team member, you will
discuss your medical history and the transplant process. You can inform them of any potential living
donors. The next part of the evaluation is physical
testing to evaluate your overall health. Imaging includes
abdominal imaging, chest X-ray, and
Cardiac testing. Bloodwork includes
Liver panels Infectious diseases panel
blood type, and other tests for overall health. Your labs can be drawn within the transplant
center health system or at a local laboratory, such as Quest or Labcorp. You will work with your coordinator to schedule
testing. If you completed these tests recently, please
inform your coordinator. Delays in work-up will result in delays in
getting listed. You should also provide documentation that
you are up to date on other health maintenance including dental evaluation and vaccines like
pneumonia, flu, COVID-19, or hepatitis, and cancer screenings like colonoscopy. For women, pap smears and mammograms. Once your evaluation is completed, the transplant
team will discuss your case at our committee meeting to determine transplant recommendations. Based on your risks versus benefits of transplant,
you will either be Approved for transplant listing,
Declined for transplant listing, or On hold for additional information Your coordinator or doctor will call you after
the meeting to discuss the recommendation. There are many reasons to be on hold, such
as additional testing, treatments, or substance abuse program participation. Please provide documentation to your coordinator
about progress or completion of these steps. If the team decides transplant is not the
best option for you, you should continue care with your liver doctor. You can have a second opinion at another transplant
center. If you are approved, you will be added to
the waitlist, and your coordinator will inform you of the next steps. If you have any questions, reach out. Your transplant team is here to support you.

caption_text:
The MedStar Georgetown Transplant
Institute is one of the leading transplant centers in the United States
in terms of volumes and outcomes. In the field of liver transplantation, we are
one of the largest centers in the region. So, we are highly experienced, and our
transplant team is really second to none. All our patients are cared for by a
thoroughly qualified multidisciplinary team that covers absolutely everything
you need as an organ donor. Your team will include the hepatologist, a surgeon,
a nurse coordinator, a social worker, a donor advocate, and a psychiatrist.
Each one is committed to guiding and supporting you through the entire
transplant process. So a living donor gives just a portion
of their liver to someone in need of a transplant. The recipient's entire
diseased liver is removed and is replaced by a piece from the donor. The
liver is the only organ in our bodies that regenerates. The donated organ grows
back to nearly full size. The donor's liver also grows back to near full size
within about eight weeks. With over fourteen thousand people waiting for a
liver transplant in the United States, there are not enough deceased donor
livers for all the patients waiting for a life-saving organ.
Unfortunately, 30% of the people on the waiting list either become too sick to
receive the transplant or pass away. So, receiving a liver from a living donor is
a real game changer and a wonderful option for some recipients. Whereas a
recipient could wait months or years for a deceased donor liver, recipients with a
living donor have a much shorter wait time. A shorter wait time means less time
for the recipient to become more sick and develop life-threatening
complications. So timing is key. You have to keep in mind that there is a window
of opportunity. Once a recipient is eligible for a living donor transplant,
they can start sharing their story and the option of receiving a transplant
from a living donor from their family members and friends. A donor must
voluntarily come forward before the recipient becomes too sick for living
donor transplant. And there are many advantages to receiving a living donor
transplant over a deceased donor transplant. Since living donors are
healthy people who have undergone extensive medical evaluation, the quality
of the liver is likely better. Because the donors and recipients surgery happen
at the same time, the period of time that the liver is outside the body and
without blood supply is a few minutes instead of hours. There are requirements for the person
donating a portion of their liver. The donor goes through a process of
evaluation and testing in order to qualify. The donor must have a compatible
or identical blood type, be in good physical and mental health, be at least
18 years old, and younger than 56 years old, understand the risk and benefits of
donation and the alternative treatments available to the recipient, and be
willing to donate voluntarily free of coercion. And it's important to know that
there is ZERO medical cost for the donor. The recipient's insurance pays for all
the living donor's medical expenses. Many of the risks involved with donating a
liver are the same as with any major surgery. Most liver donors do not
experience any complications. The complications that might occur are
usually minor. More serious complications include bleeding, blood clots in the legs
or lungs, infections, or heart problems. Risks that are more specific to liver
surgery are bile leaks or permanent liver failure requiring a liver
transplant. And although rare, the mortality rate of
living liver donors is about 0.2% or two deaths out of 1,000 donors. If you're
considering donating a portion of your liver,
remember our number one priority is your safety. We'll discuss these risks in
depth during evaluation. At any point during evaluation and even up until the
day of surgery, the donor may decide not to proceed with donation. This decision
will be respected by the living donor team. After surgery, the donor will be in the
hospital for four to seven days. This is a major abdominal surgery, so the team
will have to work to keep pain levels down. And most donors are pain free
within three weeks. You can expect to return to daily activities after four
weeks and return to work between six weeks and three months. The Transplant

caption_text: Hello and welcome to our liver transplant education program. Today we are here to guide you through some important aspects of your care after your transplant so you can stay healthy and enjoy your new life. First, let's talk about the key aspects of your post-rplant care. It is essential to understand that your body is adjusting to a new liver and this process requires ongoing monitoring and care. Here are four main areas we will focus on. Medications, lab work, clinic visits, and communication with our healthcare team. Let's start with medications. You'll be on medications called immunosuppressive medications for life as they will prevent your body from rejecting your new liver. It is important to follow your medication schedule and essential your support person helps you early in your recovery to ensure that your medications are taken correctly. Please note that any changes to your transplant medications should only be made by the transplant team. Also inform the team if any of your healthcare providers prescribe a new medication. Notify your pharmacy at least one week in advance when you need to refill as it is especially important that you do not run out of your transplant medications. Let's talk about lab work. Regular blood tests are crucial after your transplant. These tests help us monitor your liver function and check for any signs of rejection, infection, or complications. You will have labs drawn twice weekly in the beginning and then less frequently as your recovery progresses. It's important to keep all your lab appointments as they provide us with vital information about how your liver is doing. Next, let's discuss your clinic visits. You will have scheduled follow-up appointments with our transplant team. These visits will be frequent in the beginning to ensure that you are recovering well from the surgery and less so as your recovery progresses. It is vital that you stay in touch with the transplant team regarding any liver related complaints or concerns. Early intervention is key to addressing any potential issues before they become serious. You will be assigned a transplant nurse coordinator who will be your go-to team member who is available during normal business hours. We have an on call team that is available to you after hours and on the weekends that will field any urgent concerns you may have. title: How is the MELD score used for liver transplant candidates?
description: Madhavi Rudraraju, MD of Methodist Specialty and Transplant Hospital explains the purpose of the MELD score and how it is used to determine the mortality rate of an individual before making them a transplant recipient.
caption_text:
- Patients or families with
liver disease may have heard about the term, MELD Score. MELD Score was designed many years ago to predict the 90-day
mortality after a procedure called TIPS procedure which
is a shunt inside the liver. Later, they found out that
it's a very good predictor for patients with cirrhosis
and their survival or mortality and, in 2002,
they have employed this for patients being
evaluated for transplant and to decide who gets
priority for transplant. MELD Score uses four
different blood work numbers. The four different numbers
that are used are, one, bilirubin which is how
jaundice the patient is. The second number they use
is INR which is how well the blood is clotting because
liver makes clotting factors and, if the liver's sick, it
can't make clotting factors so their blood is very thin. The third number it uses
is called creatinine which is how well the kidney is working. When the liver gets very sick,
the kidneys can get hurt too and their creatinine can go up. The last number, which is the
one that was added recently to the MELD Score
calculator, is called sodium which is an electrolyte in your blood. As the liver disease advances,
patients will have low sodium in their blood. Based on these four numbers,
when you put these numbers and get a MELD Score, it
can range anywhere from five to 40 or higher. For listing purposes, anything about 40 is still listed as 40. If the MELD Score's less
than 10, the risk of dying in the next 90 days is less
than 3% which is less than three out of 100 people will
die related to complications from liver disease. Where as if their MELD Score is over 40, their risk of dying in the
next three months, or 90 days, is over 80%, so more than 80
out of 100 people will die in the next 90 days which
also emphasizes why a person with the higher MELD Score
should get transplanted because that person may not
be alive for the next organ to become available. Not always is the MELD Score predictive of how sick the patient is, so you UNOS, the organization that
allocates liver transplants, they have recognized certain
conditions to be at high risk for death though the patients
may have lower MELD Score. To name a few examples, the first one is hepatocellular
carcinoma, or liver cancer. People with liver cancer
are at increased risk of dying because the cancer can spread to other organs and
that's why it's considered as a priority for transplant and they get MELD exception points. The other condition is called
hepatopulmonary syndrome. It is a disease where the
liver affects the lung. So, they can have low
oxygen level in the blood. So, these people are
also at increased risk of the disease progressing from
the hepatopulmonary syndrome to where they don't get
enough oxygen to the organs and have risk of dying,
so they get extra points for transplant, or MELD exception points. The third condition that is commonly used is also called
portopulmonary hypertension. So, because of liver disease,
they have high pressure in the lung blood vessels
that can make them go into right heart failure. So, the heart has to
pump at higher pressures and, with time, the
right heart gets weaker and it can fail, so because
of that specific reason, these patients get extra
points for transplant only after their pressure is
controlled with medications. There are a few other reasons for people to get MELD exceptions, one
is ascites, or fluid buildup in the abdomen. If that is uncontrolled with water pills and if they cannot get a
stent procedure in the liver called the TIPS procedure. The same thing with fluid
buildup in the lungs and if it's not controlled
with a stent procedure or they cannot get a stent
procedure for any reason, they can also qualify for MELD exception. For any patient to be
listed for transplant, they have to be evaluated by
the Liver Transplant Center. The physician will first
see you and talk to you, find out your whole
history and, based on that, decide if you may benefit
from a transplant. Once all the testing is done, then your case will be discussed in a patient selection
conference which is a meeting where all the physicians, the
social workers, psychologists, all the team members that
have seen you will be there will go through all the
testing you have had and, if everything looks good, then
we decide that you're good to be placed on the transplant
list, then we submit your case to UNOS to put
you on the transplant list. (lighthearted music)

title: Decompensated Cirrhosis and Treatment With Liver Transplant
description:
Cirrhosis is a late stage of scarring (fibrosis) of the liver caused by many forms of liver diseases and conditions. Each time your liver is injured it tries to repair itself. In the process, scar tissue forms. As cirrhosis progresses, more and more scar tissue forms, making it difficult for the liver to function (decompensated cirrhosis). Advanced cirrhosis is life-threatening. The liver damage done by cirrhosis generally can't be undone.
 
Julie Heimbach, M.D., transplant surgeon and Michael Leise, M.D., transplant hepatologist, discuss decompensated cirrhosis and the treatment options available to patients when they come to Mayo Clinic.

What to Expect During Your Liver Transplant Surgery

This patient education video from UC Health, led by Dr. Cutler Quillen, Surgical Director for Liver Transplantation, walks you through the liver transplant surgery process.

🏥  Get an overview of what to expect during your transplant procedure and post-operative care.

This video prepares you for your liver transplant surgery, providing clarity and reducing anxiety about the process.
caption_text: Hello, I'm Dr. Cutler Quillin, the surgical director for liver transplantation here at UC Health. Welcome to your patient education video about your liver transplant surgery. I want to take this opportunity to walk you through what to expect with your transplant procedure and for your post-operative care. Whether you're receiving a liver transplant, simultaneous liver kidney transplant, or a living donor liver transplant, our expert team of transplant professionals are here to help you through the process every step of the way. Your goal is our goal, getting a life-saving liver transplant. Now, once you're placed on our liver transplant weight list, you'll be notified by our coordinators when a liver that's a perfect match for you becomes available. In most cases, you'll have several hours to come to the hospital, but in some instances, we need you here as soon as possible as time is of the essence. Your liver transplant surgery will take anywhere from 5 to 8 hours where your surgeons will remove the diseased liver and replace it with the healthy donor organ. During the surgery, your surgeon will make a series of blood vessel connections to restore blood flow to the liver prior to making the bile duct connection, which completes the liver transplant surgery. The expectation is that you'll need a blood transfusion during the transplant and sometimes even afterwards. Most liver transplant recipients have the breathing tube removed at the end of surgery and spend about 1 to two days in the ICU. From there, you'll be removed to the surgical floor where you'll complete the remainder of your hospitalization, which typically lasts about 8 days. Now liver transplant is a huge and complex operation. So it only makes sense that some complications can occur. In some instances we have to complete the liver transplant over the course of two operations as the field is far too bloody to safely close. In these instances the abdomen is temporarily packed. You're kept sedated and we do a planned return to the operating room once the field has dried up. Now, in other cases, you might have to undergo an unplanned return to the operating room after your initial liver transplant, which could be due to bleeding or issues with the blood vessel or bile duct connections. Be sure to talk to your liver transplant physician for more information about other potential complications that might be unique to your specific situation. If complications do occur, you can anticipate that your hospital stay might be prolonged. During your hospital stay, you'll be assessed by our multi-disiplinary care team to determine when you met appropriate milestones for a safe discharge from the hospital. Our physical and occupational therapists will work with you after your transplant to ensure you have the appropriate resources to physically thrive outside of the hospital. For some recipients, this means that you might need to be discharged to a rehab or nursing care facility to get stronger before you go home. Throughout your transplant stay, our dedicated nurse coordinator will be there with you and will meet with you and your support team to discuss what you can expect after the transplant. They will review your medications and ensure you know how to take them properly. To ensure a smooth transition upon discharge, you'll have detailed discharge instructions, including information on who you can contact 24/7 if you have any issues or questions at home. We here at UC Health are committed to your well-being every step of the way. And understand that undergoing a liver transplant is a life-changing experience. If you have any questions or concerns, please don't hesitate to reach out to our transplant team, and together we'll navigate this life-changing journey. [Music]

caption_text: ♪ Liver transplantation is considered when the liver no longer functions adequately, resulting in liver failure. However, there are more people on the transplant waiting list than livers available from deceased donors. Many patients unfortunately die or become too sick to receive a liver transplant from a deceased donor by the time one becomes available. Living donor liver transplantation is an important option for many patients on the waiting list and offers a better chance when time matters. Finding a living donor from a healthy adult shortens the waiting time to receive a liver, frees up a liver for a patient on the waiting list who does not have this option, increases long term transplant success and longer lasting livers versus deceased donors, can lower liver rejection rates, broadens availability of healthy livers for children in need, and provides convenience for the donor and recipient to schedule an optimal surgery date. A living liver owner can be a family member or friend of the recipient, or can be an anonymous donor. To become a donor candidate, you must be in good mental and physical health, have no major illnesses, including no history of fatty liver or viral hepatitis, must be between 18 and 60 years of age, and ideally, have a compatible or identical blood type with the person who is to receive the liver. If you only have a blood type incompatible donor, you and your donor can participate in the Living Donor Paired Exchange Program, where two incompatible pairs exchange living donors to receive a portion of the liver from a blood type compatible donor. All potential donors undergo a complete medical and psychosocial evaluation to ensure they meet donor qualifications. A person who is considering becoming a living liver donor needs to be physically, financially and emotionally ready to be a donor. Donating an organ is a personal decision that should only be made after becoming fully informed about its potential risks and benefits without pressure to donate. Candidates may decide at any time not to donate. Here's what happens during living donor liver transplantation. A portion of a donor's healthy liver is transplanted into a recipient in need. Living donor liver transplantation is possible because the liver, unlike any other organ in the body, has the ability to regenerate or regrow. Most regeneration of both the donor's and recipient's livers occurs within the first eight weeks. As one of the largest liver transplant programs nationally, Cleveland Clinic has pioneered and perfected the use of living donors in both pediatric and adult recipients, with outcomes among the best in the country. Donor safety is a key principle in living donor liver transplant surgery. Cleveland Clinic is also one of few hospitals worldwide to offer minimally invasive laparoscopic living donor surgery for liver transplantation in adult and pediatric recipients. This advanced procedure offers many benefits to the donor, including smaller scars, better recovery, and quicker return to normal life. For more information on finding or becoming a living liver donor, visit clevelandclinic.org/livingdonation.

title: Heart Transplants: What to Expect While Waiting & Post-Op | Cincinnati Children's
description:
http://www.cincinnatichildrens.org

Nurse Practitioner Shelly Stark gives a tour of the heart transplant process at Cincinnati Children's.

"Hi, I'm Shelly Stark, a nurse practitioner here at Cincinnati Children's hospital. I will be walking you through a tour of what it's like to go through the heart transplant process.

Waiting is often the most difficult part of the heart transplant process.
You're always wondering when that organ will come.

Wait lists and times depend on several factors, including age, weight, blood type and distance.

Frequent lab work and clinic visits may be required prior to transplant.

Remember, there is no traveling outside a 4-hour driving distance from Cincinnati Children's hospital while on the waiting list.

Also, remember to notify your provider if you're ill or having symptoms. 

We will notify you when we accept and organ. We will then give you information about when to stop eating and how to prepare for the surgery. You will then be admitted to the CICU.

Please keep in mind that once the doctors get to the donor hospital and see the donor heart, they may determine that it's not good for transplant. However, if they feel like it is good, we will move forward with the surgery.

You'll recover here, in the CICU. You can expect a lot of lines, tubes and a breathing tube. But don't be scared, this is just so the doctors can monitor you closely.

It will take you a little while to recover from surgery. You may feel nauseas and not want to eat. But that is OK. Give yourself some time, and it will improve.

You will have to be on a lot of medications, some even for the rest of your life.

Post transplant, you'll have to stay within 9 miles of Cincinnati Children's hospital for up to three months. Following that, your normal life can start to resume.

Please contact us at 513-803-2997 with any questions you may have, or visit us at http://www.cincinnatichildrens.org

title: ABO Incompatible and Positive Crossmatch Kidney Transplants
description:
Dr. Mark Stegall, Kidney and Pancreas Transplant Surgeon at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, MN, discusses antibody barriers to successful kidney transplantation.  

In some instances, kidney transplant candidates have antibodies in their bloodstream that can attack a new kidney transplant.  This can lead to antibody-mediated rejection or even loss of the transplant.  The two major types of antibodies are antibodies against the donor blood type (when incompatible) and antibodies against the donor tissue types (called HLA types or anti-HLA antibodies).

ABO incompatible kidney transplants 

Blood group antibodies occur naturally.  For example, a blood group O recipient (their cells have no blood group on their surface) commonly will have antibodies against both blood group A and B.  Thus, if a blood group O recipient has antibodies that can reject a blood group A donor kidney.   While this is a barrier to transplantation, it is relatively easy to overcome and the long-term success of these transplants is quite good.  Recently, paired donation has become another option for these donor/recipient combinations.   

Anti-HLA Antibodies: "Sensitized Patients"

HLA are "tissue types" that we talk about when we refer to a donor kidney "matching" the recipient.   Anti-HLA antibodies can be a significant barrier to transplantation and be a major contributor to both early and chronic kidney transplant loss.  Due to prior transplants, pregnancy and blood transfusions, about 30 percent of kidney transplant candidates have some type of anti-HLA antibodies. This is even more common patients undergoing their second transplant.  Patients with anti-HLA antibodies are called "sensitized patients."

I you have anti-HLA antibodies, you have several options.  You can be placed on the deceased donor list, but commonly the chance of transplantation is only about 5 percent per year.  A better option may be to be entered into our active paired donor program. In this program that includes all 3 Mayo Clinic locations, patients with antibodies against their donor can be paired with donors against whom they have little or no antibodies.  This makes the antibody barrier to transplant much easier to overcome.

In some instances, a paired donor cannot be found and we will recommend performing the kidney transplant even if there is a significant amount of anti-HLA antibody.  Over the past 14 years, Mayo Clinic Rochester has developed expertise in the development of new medicines that control antibody production or alter its impact on the transplant.  Thus, the success of these transplants are constantly improving and may be your best option for a transplant.

Options for Patients with antibodies against their donor: 
• Deceased donor waiting list 
• Paired donor program.
• Plasma exchange -- Reduces antibody levels
• Take special medications that reduce the risk of rejection

With our expertise in transplanting sensitized patients, we can give patients a wide variety of options and help you make the best decision.   

If you would like more information on this topic or would like to schedule an appointment, you may contact the Mayo Clinic Transplant Program at 1-866-249-1648 or visit our website. http://www.mayoclinic.org/kidney-transplant/

caption_text: Coronary artery bypass surgery is as the name suggests when you get a blockage in your coronary vessel. To treat that, you have two possible ways. One is to put a stent and push that narrowing or stenosis open. Another option is actually bypass it and in coronary artery bypass surgery what we do is we bypass that blockage. We leave that blockage in place, but we go beyond that blockage and feed that vessel with a new inlet. For a fresh blood supply There are three major blood vessels to supply blood to the heart, the left coronary artery, which divides into two major branches, and then the right coronary artery and patients can develop blockages in those arteries that lead to heart disease. Coronary bypass surgery is utilizing either a vein or an artery to bypass the blockages, and the bypasses are usually placed in a location that is far beyond the blockage. Thereby not only treating the blockage that's occurring at present, but also treating future blockages for most patients. You do as many bypasses as necessary to achieve what's called a complete revascularization, meaning that you have bypassed every single significant or sizable vessel to all major territories of the heart. Cleveland Clinic, for the most part invented coronary bypass surgery. Back in the 1960s Mason Stones was a cardiologist who happened upon coronary angiography and developed really the the first coronary angiogram. And together with his surgical colleague, Brene Favaro they worked and were able to do the first coronary bypass and coronary bypass surgery. Had a tremendous history here at the Cleveland Clinic from the early 1970s. We did far more coronary bypass surgeries here than anywhere else in the world. Coronary artery bypass surgery is certainly the most common operation that heart surgeons perform and it's actually the most common operation among heart surgery programs in the country. But that doesn't mean that it's the same operation for every patient. Every patient needs a tailored approach to coronary revascularization. So there are multiple approaches for coronary artery bypass surgery. The standard approach is utilizing a full sternotomy which is full splitting of the sternum and the surgery can be performed either utilizing the heart lung machine or what's called off pump technique. And thereby we use stabilizers to stabilize portions of the heart to do the bypasses we need to do. We can also perform minimally invasive coronary bypass surgery. A lot of those can be performed through a very small incision between the ribs. We never wanna compromise quality for cosmetics because our objective is not to have a perfect immediate outcome. Our objective is to have long-term success. When we look at performing bypass surgery we use either the mammary artery, a radial artery from the arm or a portion of the saphenous vein from the leg. Now, each of these bypasses lasts certain length of time. They don't last forever. The mammary artery by far lasts the longest. It's one of the only arteries in the body that really does not develop atherosclerosis. So multi arterial grafting is by far the best strategy for performing coronary artery bypasses for patients because it gives the most long lasting effect. Not only do we have high volume cardiac surgery practice but the patients we get here are very high risk patients. We accept patients from all over the country, in fact from all over the world. Many of them have seen one two or more surgeons that have declined to offer those patients surgery because of their high risk. And the surgeons here are very comfortable dealing with those patients. The Cleveland Clinic has long been a leader in reoperative coronary artery bypass surgery that is new coronary bypasses in someone who's had bypass surgery before. We do the largest number of those cases yearly than any other center. What we do to achieve excellent results is having a great team approach. We have excellent surgeons, we have excellent support and we use grafts and techniques that ensure that the patient will have not only excellent short-term outcomes and very low complication rate but also excellent long-term results. I think a lot of patients before heart surgery don't actually fully understand how poorly they feel and what's rewarding is seeing them return to what they were seeing them really be able to enjoy life again. ♪

title: Shorter patients are less likely to receive lung transplants
description:
Short people have several health advantages over tall people, including lower risk for cancer and heart disease, and longer life expectancy. But there’s at least one health-related downside to being small: the odds of getting a lung transplant are considerably lower.

Are you thinking about lung transplantation for yourself or your loved one? Some patients living with pulmonary fibrosis may be eligible for a lung transplant, but it is a complex process that may not be right for everyone with PF.

Dr. Marie Budev, Medical Director of Lung Transplantation at the Cleveland Clinic, recommends that patients remain positive, and stay as healthy and active as possible during the waiting period. The path and timing is different for each individual so it is important to remember that every day counts.

title: Living Donor Liver Transplant
description:
UChicago Medicine transplant surgeon Dr. John LaMattina explains adult living donor liver transplantation in this animated video. Living donor liver transplantation is an option for patients with end-stage liver disease or liver failure. A liver from a living donor is an alternative to the long organ waiting list, and a faster path to transplant. The living donor's liver and the recipient's new piece of liver will fully regrow and function normally within a few months of transplant. Dr. LaMattina also reviews the requirements for a living liver donor and explains the surgeries. 

Learn more: https://www.uchicagomedicine.org/conditions-services/transplant/liver-transplant/living-donor-liver-transplant

description:
After a liver transplant, your child will need special ongoing care, including testing, medication adjustments, regular check-up and follow-ups into adulthood.

Information on Slides in the Video

If you have blood type O you can receive a kidney from a donor with the blood type O, and donate a kidney to any blood type
If you have blood type A you can receive a kidney from a donor with the blood types A or O, and donate a kidney to someone with a blood type of A or AB

Blood Type O is the most common with 45% of the US population, type A is 40% of the population, type B is 10%, and type AB is 5%

If a donor kidney is from a patient with an incompatible blood type, and the recipient isn't desensitized then two issues could happen:
Hemolytic transfusion reaction - recipient ABO antibody reacts with donor RBC and activates C', resulting in the desctruction of transfused RBCs
Hyperacute rejection - recipient ABO antibodies react with donor ABO antigens. C' is activated at the surgace of endothelial cells, resulting in rapid destruction of the cells.

Survival rates lower than ABOc, but promising results
20 years later - widespread adoption in Europe
2005 - 2012: 1420 Living Donor ABOi
Varying desensitization and IS protocols
Overall graft survival at 3 years comparable to ABOc

All ABOi pairs are entered into KPD
Baseline anti-ABO titer
Insurance must agree to pay for desensitization
Careful informed consent from donor and recipient
Begin desensitization protocol

Begin immunosuppression

Measure anti-ABO titer daily x2 weeks post

PP/IVIG for AMR

Increase incidence AMR 1-28 days post
3-year graft survival same as ABOc

title: Livers Donated after Cardiac Death are Safe to Use in Liver Cancer Patients on a Transplant List
description:
Patients with liver cancer can be cured with a liver transplant. But because of the shortage of donated organs, these patients often die waiting for a liver. That’s because most transplant centers predominantly use livers from donors who die from brain death.
But in the largest study of its kind, transplant physicians at Mayo Clinic in Florida have found that liver cancer patients have the same beneficial outcomes using organs donated by patients who died of cardiac death. The study was recently published online in the American Journal of Transplantation.  Lead author, Dr. Kristopher Croome has more on the study.

title: How the national organ transplant waiting list works
description:
The shortage of organs causes most patients to wait for a transplant. Waiting times vary widely for many reasons. Contrary to popular belief, waiting for a transplant is not like taking a number and waiting your turn. In some respects, even the word “list” is misleading because the list is really a giant pool of patients. When a deceased organ donor is identified, UNOS’ computer system generates a ranked list of transplant candidates who are suitable to receive each organ. Matching is the key to connecting individuals waiting for a lifesaving transplant with compatible donor organs. Explore other FAQs about organ donation & transplantation:
https://unos.org/transplant/frequently-asked-questions/

description:

"Hi. Welcome to the Heart Institute at Cincinnati Children's. My name is Breann Taylor. I am a heart transplant pharmacist here at the hospital.

I'm going to walk you through the expected follow-up visits after your heart transplant.

Our goal is to make sure you have the best quality of life after surgery. You will have the highest risk for rejection or an acute event in the first year. There will be some restrictions at first, but as time goes on, those restrictions will become less and less.

Come take a walk with me, and we will check out the clinic where you will have your follow-ups.

You will be seen in clinic every week for the first three months after transplant. I know this seems like a lot, but this is a crucial time for us to monitor your progress.

If everything progresses according to plan, these visits will become further and further apart.

During these visits, you will have an echocardiogram so that we will have a better understanding of how your body is reacting to your new heart.

After transplant, you will be taking several new medications. It is very important to take these medications exactly as directed by the heart transplant team. This will help ensure that your body does not reject your new heart.

It is very important to make sure your labs are drawn at the right time. In order for us to make sure your levels are within goal, labs should be drawn 30 to 60 minutes before your next dose is due.

Keeping your primary care physician after transplant is very important. This person will be responsible for treating any illness not related to the heart, as well as for your yearly checkup.

Communication with your transplant team about labs, medication and illness is key to a successful recovery.

Please call our office at 513-803-2997. We're here to answer any questions you may have.

Severe lung damage has been a serious outcome for COVID-19 patients who survive and face recovery from the disease.

"As we know, lungs are one of the major organs that are involved with COVID infection," says Dr. Sadia Shah, a Mayo Clinic transplant pulmonologist and critical care physician. She says that, in the future, these are the patients who may need a lung transplant.

title: Pediatric Liver Transplant Recovery in the Hospital
description:
Learn about what to expect during and immediately after your child’s liver transplant at Children’s Hospital Colorado. This video discusses recovery and describes the medical devices we use following a pediatric liver transplant and why we use them. 
Understanding the instruments and devices we use during and after a pediatric liver transplant and why we use them will help both you and your child be better prepared to recover in the hospital. Following your child’s liver transplant, it’s important that we can easily monitor them and run tests as they recover and their body gets used to its new liver. Watch the video to understand how we help your child recovery safely and effectively after a liver transplant. 
For more information about pediatric liver transplants, visit https://www.childrenscolorado.org/doctors-and-departments/departments/transplant/liver/ 

Connect with Children’s Colorado: 
Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/childrenscolo  
Facebook: https://www.facebook.com/childrenshospitalcolorado  
Twitter: https://twitter.com/ChildrensColo 
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/company/children's-hospital-colorado  
Website: http://www.childrenscolorado.org
caption_text:
In this video, we’ll be going over what
to expect during and immediately after a liver transplant surgery at Children’s Hospital
Colorado. A liver transplant is a very complicated surgery,
which tends to involve several tubes, drains, and overall monitoring. Before the surgery begins, your child will
be given general anesthesia, so they will not feel any pain during the procedure. After anesthesia and before the surgery starts,
anesthesiologists will place a central venous catheter in the internal jugular vein for
close monitoring of your child’s overall fluid status during the transplant. After the procedure, nurses will use this
catheter to easily draw blood. An arterial line will also be placed for close
monitoring of your child’s blood pressure and heart rate. Another catheter placed before the operation
begins is called a Foley catheter, which is a flexible tube that passes through the urethra
and into the bladder to drain urine. At the end of the liver transplant, the surgeons
will place one or more JP drains near the liver to monitor for bleeding or bile leakage. JP drains are closed-suction devices which
collect bodily fluids from surgical sites. They will look at the bulb to monitor for
bleeding (red fluid) or bile leaking (green fluid). After the liver transplant is done, your child
will be taken to the pediatric intensive care unit or PICU. Here the nurses will perform frequent labs
and monitor your child and the surgeons will remain in constant communication with the
PICU team. An ultrasound of the new liver will be done
when your child arrives and every morning for the first 5 days after the liver transplant. There are occasions where your child may need
to be on a ventilator after the transplant or may need hemodialysis. These are both temporary measures and will
be stopped as soon as possible. Your child will usually begin to eat and drink
1-3 days after the transplant, depending on how the surgeons connected the bile duct. JP drains can be removed at bedside as soon
as the surgical team is comfortable. Usually starting around 5 days after liver
transplant. For more information about liver transplants,
please watch our Liver Transplant video.

title: Kidney Transplant: The Importance of Nutrition
description: Kidney Transplant: The Importance of Nutrition, featuring Ashley Pena Elsbernd, MS, RD, LD, CNSC. From a seven-part video series that aims to share information on kidney transplantation at UT Southwestern.
caption_text: I'm Ashley Pena Elsbernd. I'm a transplant dietician here at UT Southwestern, and I'll be talking about Nutrition and Transplant. First, the importance of nutrition and transplant is that nutrition plays a really important role before and after transplant. To get you ready for transplant, we wanna make sure that your body is in the best shape or condition that it can be. And that means controlling any preexisting conditions that you may have, like higher blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, but also making sure to maintain a healthy body weight. After transplant, it's important to have a good nutrition because it can help impact your recovery and also long-term health maintenance. For recovery, good nutrition can promote wound healing and prevent infection. Long-term after transplant, good nutrition can help control high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes and weight gain that tend to be common side effects associated with the transplant medications. To decrease your risk of heart disease and high blood cholesterol and triglycerides, you'll want to follow a heart healthy diet. The principles of the heart healthy diet include limiting foods with added fats, added salt and added sugar. An added benefit of the heart healthy diet is it can help maintain or control your weight. What does a heart healthy diet look like? First, we wanna reduce our intake of foods that contain saturated fats. A diet high in saturated fat can contribute to elevated LDL or bad blood cholesterol levels, increasing your risk for cardiovascular disease or stroke. Foods high in saturated fat tend to be animal-based products like fatty cuts of meat, poultry skin, bacon, sausage and whole fat dairy products like whole milk, cream, yogurt, cheeses and butter. A good visualization for saturated fats is they tend to be solid at room temperature. So that would include coconut oil and palm oils as well. The other type of fat you'll want to limit are trans fats, which are found in a lot of packaged and processed foods. Trans fats can raise your LDL or bad blood cholesterol and decrease your HDL or good blood cholesterol, increasing your risk for cardiovascular disease. To identify trans fats in foods, read the ingredients list for partially hydrogenated oils and do your best to eliminate any foods that have these ingredients. So what's allowed on the heart healthy diet? It's really important to choose your lean cuts of meat, so eating more chicken, fish, turkey more often than some of the higher fat meats like beef and pork. You'll also wanna choose lower fat dairy products like skim milk or 1% milk. The other thing you'll want to increase in your diet is the omega-3 fats. Omega-3 fats can reduce your triglyceride levels and may help improve your HDL or good blood cholesterol levels. Omega-3 fats are found in cold ocean fast-swimming fish like tuna, salmon, mackerel, but also in some plant-based products like flaxseed or flaxseed oil and walnuts. Finally, you'll wanna make sure you have a diet high in fiber. Fiber in foods can help lower your LDL or bad blood cholesterol. Fiber in foods are gonna be in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, dried beans and legumes. Now, in order to help control high blood pressure, hypertension, and even help control fluid retention on your body, you'll wanna follow a low sodium diet. Low sodium means anywhere from 1,500 to 2,000 milligrams of sodium per day. To put that into perspective, one teaspoon of table salt has 2,300 milligrams of sodium. So the best way to lower sodium in your diet is to take that salt shaker off the table, but also to season your foods with herbs, spices and seasonings that are sodium-free. Fresh herbs or dried herbs are gonna be lowest in sodium. caption_text: My name is SueAnn Delecato. I am a registered dietician at Albany Medical Center for the kidney transplant program. I would like to take a few minutes to talk about diet and nutrition after a kidney transplant. There are four topics that I will be discussing, including following a more liberalized and heart healthy diet after transplant. By liberalized I mean no longer needing to restrict potassium and phosphorous in your diet. Sometimes these are what people with kidney failure have to follow before transplant. This is only of course if your new kidney is working properly. I will also discuss the importance of following general food safety guidelines after transplant to prevent foodborne illness. Avoiding herbs, botanicals, grapefruit and pomegranate juice will also be discussed briefly. Keeping your heart healthy is important in general and especially after a kidney transplant. Following a heart healthy diet includes eating less salt if your blood pressure is or remains high, and sometimes medications can cause your blood pressure to be high and sometimes cause fluid retention as well. Avoiding high fat, greasy food and junk foods. This will help keep your weight and cholesterol levels under control. Some transplant medications can cause cholesterol and triglyceride levels to rise also. Eat fruits and vegetables daily. Fruits and vegetables have natural fibers in them which can help keep you regulated, control cholesterol levels, and keep you feeling full longer. Many fruits and vegetables are also known to contain antioxidants that can help prevent cancer. Foodborne infections are a common and sometimes life-threatening concern for millions of people. For those that are immunocompromised, for example after a kidney transplant, the risk of foodborne infection may be high. For this reason we at Albany Medical Center recommend following some basic food safety recommendations to reduce your risk of infection and illness. These recommendations are especially important during the first few months after your transplant when you are most likely to be on high doses of immunosuppression medications. Some general guidelines to follow include avoiding raw meats and fish, making sure you cook your meat until it's no longer pink inside. Hard cook or scramble your eggs, no runny yolks. Fruit and vegetables that you intend to eat raw should be washed with a vinegar and water mixture. Generally a recipe of one part vinegar to three parts water will do the trick. Rinse your vegetables and fruits after you rinse them with the vinegar and water mixture and then consume them. If your fruits and vegetables are cooked you shouldn't have a problem 'cause that should be able to kill the bacteria if there's any on them. Avoid buffets and salad bars. These places are breeding grounds for bacteria. Wash your hands when preparing foods, washing cutting boards, and countertops well. If you have well water, the Environmental Protection Agency recommends that you have your water tested regularly for contaminants and bacteria. City water and bottled water are generally considered safe to drink. If you are taking, or considering taking, herbal or botanical supplements, it is recommended that you don't. Some may increase the risk of organ rejection, such as ginseng and echinacea, and others may cause a drug interaction with transplant medications you are taking. St. John's Wort is another example. Finally, both grapefruit and pomegranate juice can alter the effects of your transplant medications as well. We therefore recommend that you avoid these products too. In summary, most kidney transplant patients can enjoy a more liberalized diet after transplant. Please keep in mind that following general food safety recommendations will decrease your chances of contracting a foodborne illness while taking immunosuppression medications, especially during the first few months after transplant. Eating a well-balanced diet which includes fruits and vegetables will keep your body healthy and prevent unwanted weight gain. Avoiding excessive salt intake, high fat foods, and junk foods will also keep your blood pressure, cholesterol, and blood sugar under good control.

Mayo Clinic Minute - What to expect as a living kidney donor
For those with kidney failure, the wait for a new kidney can take years. There just are not enough organs from deceased donors to fill the need. Fortunately, a person can live a healthy life with just one kidney, making living-donor kidney transplants an alternative to deceased-donor transplants. title: Side effects from corticosteroids
description: Corticosteroids, also known as steroids, are medications that are commonly prescribed by doctors to treat asthma, colds, allergies and more. Often it is used as an injection (shot). However, research shows that steroids are usually not the best option to treat these conditions. Learn more at https://www.ochsner.org/steroids
caption_text:
Corticosteroids more generally known simply as 
steroids have been given to millions of patients   since the 1940s. Modern medical best practices 
support using steroids as an anti-inflammatory   medication to treat flare-ups of conditions like 
asthma and some types of arthritis. It's important   to understand that despite their common use 
steroids can cause serious risks. Two of the most   common ways that steroids can be taken have the 
potential to produce very negative side effects   one way is through pills taken orally 
the second way is with a needle injection   many people don't realize that steroid injections 
may potentially leave behind permanent disfiguring   features known as dimpling or fat atrophy at 
the injection site usually given on the buttocks   this unsightly condition is irreversible. Another 
side effect from steroid use is an increase in   blood sugar which may pose serious problems 
particularly to patients who already have diabetes   after taking steroids patients may even experience 
increased anxiety jitters and sleepless nights for   as long as two weeks and for the next one to two 
months the chances of bone fractures, blood clots   weight gain, joint necrosis, and 
infections are dramatically increased   the irony is that patients often take steroids to 
combat infection yet the steroid itself actually   weakens the immune system this contradiction 
highlights an important fact about steroids   despite their widespread use to treat a variety 
of symptoms and illnesses the prescription of   steroids is frequently not supported by scientific 
studies and not recommended by current best   practices. Although commonly believed steroids will 
not shorten the time it takes to feel better from   sinus infections, allergies, bronchitis, colds, or the 
flu. Other types of treatments are more effective   in alleviating symptoms from these conditions 
with fewer possible side effects. In a particularly   tragic case of complications from steroids, a woman 
ended her own life in 2003 after being prescribed   a high dose steroid treatment to combat back pain. 
It's since been found that such high doses induce   psychiatric symptoms including depression, panic, 
and suicidal behavior in one out of five patients   most concerning is that suicidal behavior is six 
times more frequent in those patients who have   taken steroids compared to similar patients who 
have not. For both patients and medical providers   it's important to seriously consider whether 
the risks involved with taking steroids are   really worth it. Is the patient suffering from a 
condition that legitimately calls for steroid use? Does research-based best practices recommend 
using steroids to treat the illness or condition?  Are there less risky alternatives to steroids? 
Might over-the-counter drugs like Tylenol or   Ibuprofen be effective. At first glance, it may 
seem like steroids could be a quick fix for   someone's discomfort. However, it's important to 
remember that steroids may actually do more harm   than good. Steroids simply may not be the 
answer. Ochsner Health System is committed   to protecting our patients by prescribing 
steroids when it makes sense to do so.   Patient health is our priority and steroids should 
only be used when the benefits outweigh the risks.   For more information about the benefits and 
risks of steroids, visit ochsner.org/steroids.

title: Mayo Clinic Minute - Dual procedure combines liver transplant, bariatric surgery
description:
Mayo Clinic surgeons have found that an innovative approach can help patients with obesity get lifesaving care. Obesity can be a barrier to liver transplant. In a recent study, Dr. Julie Heimbach, director of the Mayo Clinic Transplant Center in Rochester, Minnesota, found that combining gastric sleeve surgery with liver transplantation was effective in addressing both health issues.
This dual procedure is especially helpful for patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), formerly known as nonalcoholic fatty liver disease. MASLD happens when fat builds up in the liver, often without symptoms. It's mostly caused by obesity — defined as a body mass index (BMI) of 30 or higher. In advanced stages, MASLD can lead to serious liver damage that requires a transplant.

title: Kidney Transplant Evaluation Process
description:
Welcome to the patient education video series from UC Health's transplant team. This video is designed to demystify the transplant evaluation process, providing a detailed overview of what to expect and how we determine if transplantation is the right option for you.

This video covers:
• Multi-Disciplinary Team Consultation: Learn about the initial meeting with our team and how they determine the necessary evaluation tests.

• The Evaluation Process: Understand the comprehensive nature of the medical testing and consultations, including blood work, infectious disease screenings, EKG, echocardiogram, and other specialized tests based on your medical history.

• Specialized Testing and Screenings: Find out about additional cardiac and pulmonary tests, CT scans for vascular evaluation, cancer screenings, and dental checks that are part of the evaluation.

• Selection Committee Review: Discover how your medical history and test results are reviewed by a selection committee consisting of our multi-disciplinary team to assess your suitability for transplantation.

• Understanding Contraindications: Gain insights into conditions that may pose challenges to transplantation, including active infections, cancers, substance abuse, smoking, obesity, lack of support, insurance issues, uncontrolled diabetes, and medical or surgical instability.

• Importance of Compatibility in Transplantation: We discuss how we follow a compatibility table for matching donors and recipients and explain the role of blood types and exchange programs.

• The Role of Communication and Cooperation: Emphasize the importance of staying in regular contact with our team to ensure smooth scheduling and updates throughout the evaluation process.

This video is a comprehensive guide for anyone undergoing the transplant evaluation process at UC Health. It's designed to provide clarity and understanding, ensuring that you are well-informed and comfortable with each step of the journey. If you have any questions, our team is here to support and guide you.

>> Your evaluation appointment today will
take approximately five to six hours. You have already had your labs drawn and
your chest x-ray, following this video, you will go to the clinic where you will have an
EKG, have your picture taken and you will meet with members of the transplant team. It is important to understand that no
patient is ever listed for transplant on the day of their evaluation appointment. There are several more steps to the
process before anyone could be listed. The evaluation process is an
opportunity for the transplant team to assess whether transplantation may be
beneficial to you and an opportunity for you to assess whether transplantation
is right for you. You will meet with the following members of the
transplant team during your evaluation today; the transplant nephrologist specializes
in kidney disease and will focus on assessing your overall health
in preparation for a transplant; the transplant surgeon specializes in
performing kidney and pancreas transplants and will determine whether the
operation can be performed safely on you; the social worker specializes in helping
patients and their families understand and cope with the issues they may face
related to transplantation; your transplant coordinator facilitates
your journey through the transplant process. You will also have access to a financial
coordinator who will assist you in understanding and facilitating the financial aspects of
transplantation and your insurance coverage. After all the testing results are
obtained, your case will be reviewed by the transplant evaluation committee. The committee includes the nephrologists,
the surgeons, the social workers, the financial coordinators,
dieticians, pharmacists, living donor advocate and
the transplant coordinators. All listing decisions are made by
this committee which meets each week. The committee will review your case and
make one of the following decisions; continue the evaluation process; do
not list; or list for transplant. Following the transplant
evaluation committee meeting, your transplant coordinator will write a letter
to advise you of the committee's decision and notify you of the next steps to take. You should receive this letter within
two weeks following the meeting. If you do not receive the letter, please
contact your transplant coordinator. You may receive a letter advising you the team
requires additional testing before they can make a recommendation on whether you
meet the listing qualifications. In addition to the letter, your transplant
coordinator may contact you by phone to explain the results and the
additional testing you need and answer any questions you may have. The letter will include the
specific testing you will need to complete before the committee
can review your case again. The letter will also include
the contact information where you should have the testing results faxed. You may also be contacted by your
social worker regarding social goals to complete prior to being listed. Once the results from the
additional testing are received, your case will be reviewed
again by the committee. Another letter will be sent to you following
the review of your case notifying you of the final decision and any
steps that should be taken. You may receive a letter that indicates
your records were reviewed by the committee and our team feels that a kidney and or
pancreas transplant is not in your best interest and does not recommend you proceed with
transplantation, while this may be disappointing to learn, it is important to remember the
committee only advises transplantation when it appears it will benefit
and not harm the patient. You may receive a letter indicating that
you meet all the listing qualifications and are being listed for a
deceased donor organ transplant, the letter will include all the
information you need to remain in an active status on the wait list. It will be very important to keep
your transplant coordinator informed about any changes in your life that may
impact your listing and or transplant, these may include changes in your address,
phone numbers, insurance, health conditions, hospital admissions, surgeries,
accidents and or blood transfusions.

[ Silence ] >> On the day of discharge, you
will be focused on, let's go home. While we do our best to help you accomplish your
discharge efficiently, it is important for you to know that there are many processes that
must be completed before you can go home. The staff must be sure that you have a 30 day
supply of medications before you are discharged. Your inpatient lab tests are completed. The lab tests for your first outpatient
clinic appointment are prepared, and that your follow-up appointments
to the clinic are made. The staff must review discharge
instructions with you prior to your departure. Patients who travel long distances to get home
may want to stay in a local hotel the night of discharge, since discharges may occur
late in the afternoon or early evening. Patients should make plans to have someone stay
with them to provide around the clock support for the first weeks after going home. Recipients will return to the clinic for
their first appointment after surgery within a few days after discharge, and will
visit the clinic weekly for the first six weeks. Each recipient will have an
individualized clinic visit schedule based on their needs after the first six weeks. Blood draws will need to be done twice weekly
for the first three months after discharge. The total surgical recovery
period is six to eight weeks. Recipients will need to plan transportation to their clinic appointments during
their surgical recovery period. In order to diagnose rejection of the
transplant before irreparable damage occurs, we do frequent biopsies in the
first year following transplant. A biopsy will be performed in the operating room
at the time of transplant, and then at three, six and 12 months after transplant. A biopsy requires a needle puncture in
the area of the transplanted kidney. It is important for patients to understand
that we are bound by the regulations set forth in the Health Insurance Portability
and Accountability Act or HIPPA. We cannot share your medical
information with anyone without your expressed written permission. We cannot tell your spouse, father,
mother, sister, brother, daughter, son, friend or neighbor anything. We cannot answer any questions
from the donor about the recipient. We cannot answer any question from
the recipient about the donor. If you want us to be able to talk about
your medical care with another person, you need to sign an authorization
that we will keep on file. You are not listed on the
day of your evaluation. You will only be listed when you have
completed all the requested testing, your case has been reviewed by the
transplant evaluation committee, and it has determined you meet
all the criteria for listing. You will know you are listed
when you receive a letter from your coordinator informing you the
committee has made the decision to list. You should receive a letter within two weeks of the evaluation meeting
stating what the next steps are. If you do not, please contact

description: Kidney Transplant: The Basics of Finance, featuring Scott Bennett, MS. From a seven-part video series that aims to share information on kidney transplantation at UT Southwestern.
caption_text: (bright music) I'm Scott Bennett, Associate Vice President of Solid Organ Transplant at UT Southwestern. I'm here to talk to you about the basics of transplant finance and the role of the transplant financial coordinator, better known as the TFC. The transplant financial coordinator, or TFC, is a valuable resource to help you navigate the process of transplantation. It'll help you navigate the evaluation, the waitlist, the transplant, and the post-transplant period to ensure you have a successful outcome. Our financial coordinators will verify your coverage and eligibility at various points along the transplant journey at the point of application, at the point in which our transplant team approves you for the waitlist and while you're on the waitlist to maintain readiness at all times for that transplant event. At the time in which our transplant team approves you to be placed on the waitlist and throughout the time on the waitlist to ensure the insurance company remains in approval of your transplant proceeding. It's very important to notify the transplant financial coordinator if there are any changes in your coverage or eligibility. Failure to do so could interrupt your coverage, which could impact your ability to receive a transplant. Medicare is a federal government insurance program designed to help those over 65 years of age, those who have been disabled for two years or more and those who have end-stage renal disease, or ESRD. Due to the ESRD entitlement, many patients on dialysis have Medicare. If the patient is on hemodialysis, there is a three month waiting period before entitlement begins. If the patient is on peritoneal dialysis, that waiting period is waived. And if a patient is not on dialysis yet, that's called a preemptive transplant and that waiting period is also waived. If you're currently on group healthcare insurance, most companies observe a 30 month coordination to benefit period. After the 30 month period is expired, your Medicare will become primary and your group coverage will actually become secondary at that point. UT Southwestern is a Medicare approved transplant facility. Medicare coverage comes in three parts. Part A coverage covers inpatient medical services in the hospital. Part B coverage covers outpatient hospital physician and immunosuppressant drug charges up to 80% of Medicare allowable rates. Medicare Part D covers non-immunosuppressant drugs and your cost will vary based on the plan you choose. When traditional Medicare is your only coverage, UT Southwestern requires you as a patient to have Parts A, B and D in order to be eligible for transplant. If you do not have Medicare prior to transplant, your social worker will discuss the option of accepting Medicare at the time of transplant as an option. There are other Medicare alternatives such as Medicare supplements or Medigap plans and Medicare Advantage plans. Medicare supplements help to cover costs of Medicare that aren't covered under traditional benefits such as copays, deductibles and drug costs. Patients under age 65 are limited in the number of Medigap plans or supplement plans that they are able to obtain. There are now many Medicare Advantage plans to choose from. Medicare Advantage plans are private insurance plans that are contracted directly with Medicare to provide care. Although UT Southwestern is a Medicare approved facility, UT Southwestern is not in network with all Medicare Advantage plans, so please contact your TFC before making any insurance changes. COBRA coverage is offered when you have a gap in employment. Although it's the same coverage that was once offered by your employer, it's often costly and limited in timeframe. If you are on COBRA, speak to your TFC about options to reduce your cost or extend the term of your COBRA coverage. COBRA premiums are your responsibility. Your employer will no longer be paying a portion of your premiums as they once were. It is critical as a patient that you make timely premium payments in order to ensure that there is no lapse in coverage. Patients who generously offer to be evaluated for kidney donation are not responsible for the evaluation, hospitalization or post-transplant follow-up for their care. Living donor transplant finance is complex, but in general, most living donor related services are billed to the recipient. Depending on the recipient's insurance, they may not cover the rare instance of donor-related complications. Medicare, however, does cover donation-related complications. Living donor related costs are another example of an advantage for taking Medicare when you have a qualifying event. Prospective living organ donors may be eligible for financial assistance to help cover travel costs. Check with your social worker for more information. To prevent your body from rejecting your new organ, you will have to take immunosuppressive drugs or anti-rejection drugs in addition to a variety of other medications to ensure the life of your organ. Many of these medications are very expensive. Without medication coverage, they can range anywhere from 5,000 to $7,000 a month in out-of-pocket expense. It is vital that you maintain adequate coverage to cover these expenses or maintain the resources to cover the out-of-pocket expense for your medications. Our social workers are also available to help with medication assistance programs where you may qualify. Reach out to your social worker for more information if you find yourself unable to afford medications. Any variation from your prescribed medication regimen can be detrimental to your transplant health. Once you have a better understanding of what your insurance covers, you'll have a better understanding of your responsibilities as a patient financially. Out-of-pocket medical and non-medical expenses that you should anticipate for the future include copays, deductibles and premiums for your insurance coverage, transportation to and from the transplant center, parking at the transplant center itself, temporary lodging for family and friends during and after the transplant event, potential loss of income while out of work for the transplant and childcare costs. Having a good understanding of your coverage and benefits and working closely with your transplant financial coordinator will help to ensure a successful transplant outcome. (bright music)
