title: Kidney Transplant: Hospital Course, What to expect when the transplant happens
description: Kidney Transplant: Hospital Course, featuring Parisa A. Vagefi, M.D., FACS. From a seven-part video series that aims to share information on kidney transplantation at UT Southwestern.
caption_text: (gentle music) Hi, I am Parsia Vagefi. I'm Chief of Surgical Transplantation at UT Southwestern. Today I'm gonna talk to you about what to expect for your kidney transplant. For a deceased donor kidney transplantation these can occur on any day or at any time. Well, often you'll receive a phone call from one of our coordinators and they'll notify you that you are up for a kidney transplant. This call can come at any day or time and thus you should always have your phone available and a backup phone number listed with one of our coordinators just in case you're not able to answer your phone. The coordinator will discuss with you the organ offer and also we'll let you know any pertinent information in terms of when you should arrive at the hospital, when your last food or drink should be and whether or not you should proceed to dialysis at your own center prior to coming into the hospital. They'll also give you a time to arrive to the hospital where you'll go through the admission process and be brought up to our transplant floor. Once on the floor you'll have all of the standard preoperative testing including blood work, a chest x-ray, an EKG, and also you'll meet the team and sign your surgical consent form. Bear in mind that there is some final testing that has to be done between both the donor and the recipient to make sure that the kidney is compatible and this will be performed while you're waiting to have your kidney transplant. Once the testing is complete and we know that there's full compatibility and we know that the kidney is a good quality kidney as assessed by our team, then we'll proceed to the operating room for the kidney transplant. There is a possibility that you're brought into the hospital for the kidney transplant and the testing is positive or on biopsy the kidney is not suitable for transplant and then you would be discharged home without the kidney transplant and we would hope to have you be brought back at a soon date thereafter to get a better quality kidney transplant. If you do proceed to kidney transplant the operation usually takes about three to four hours. Your old kidneys are left in place most often unless there's an indication to remove them such as an infection or a mass or a history of bleeding from the kidneys. But most often we leave your native kidneys in place. The transplanted kidney is placed in the right lower quadrant most often or sometimes on the left side if there's been previous surgery on the right side. We hook up the new kidney's blood vessels to the blood vessels that run through the leg and most often we place the urine tube that drains the kidney right into your own bladder so that you'll be able to urinate normally following transplant. Sometimes a small stent is placed to protect that new connection between the ureter and the bladder and that stent is removed in the office as an outpatient three to four weeks following the transplant. Immediately after surgery you'll go to the recovery room and from there you'll be transported back up to the surgical transplant floor. Most patients stay in the hospital for three nights following their kidney transplant. The function of the kidney can vary. Some kidneys are slow to produce urine whereas others can produce urine right away and this will be carefully assessed by the inpatient team. An assessment will be made on a daily basis whether or not any further dialysis is needed while the kidney is recovering from the transplant procedure. In the recovery period you'll be encouraged to begin walking early after surgery the following day and your diet will be slowly advanced from liquids to solid foods. In addition, you'll meet with various members of the transplant team to start learning all of your new medications as well as your dietary restrictions for an anticipated discharge on the third post-operative day. At the time of discharge you'll complete the educational process on the day of discharge and then you'll be given all of the appointments that you'll need in the post-operative period. This will include usually visiting a lab twice a week to obtain lab values and visiting the clinic at least once a week in order to assess your progress and also assess whether any further dialysis is needed while the kidney regains full function. During this time period, your labs will be closely monitored and any medications will be adjusted based upon your lab values. It is very important that you maintain your lab appointments as well as your doctor appointments in this post-operative period. As a kidney gains further function and you begin to recover further from the surgery, these appointments and lab visits will be spread out further and further. As mentioned, some patients have a stent placed to connect the ureter to the bladder. This will be arranged to be removed as an outpatient approximately three to four weeks after the surgery and this will be done in the office by the urology team. It is important that you have a support structure in place following surgery for at least two to four weeks as you will be recovering and will need assistance with such daily task as grocery shopping, driving to appointments and driving to lab visits. As mentioned, as you gain back your strength you'll be able to function more independently as time passes. Usually by one month after surgery people are fully independent again as they were prior to surgery. Most patients are discharged directly to home following the kidney transplant. Many of our patients come from far distances. If this is the case, we have an excellent team of social workers that can assist in finding you temporary lodging in the DFW area so that you can maintain your lab visits and clinic visits in the immediate post-operative period until you are safe to return to your home. What are the risks associated with the transplant surgery? As mentioned, not all kidneys function immediately. Therefore, there is a chance of what we call delayed graph function where you will require dialysis in the post-operative period within the first seven days and sometimes this may extend into your recovery while at home. Do not worry. Our nephrologists work very well with your outpatient nephrology team and will set up dialysis at your local dialysis center until the kidney is fully recovered. In addition, our nephrologist will work with you to maintain your diabetes, your high blood pressure, and any other medical illnesses under good control in the post-operative period. We have an excellent transplant pharmacy team which will go over all of your medications while you're in the hospital and ensure that you're on all the right medications when you return home. Other risks associated with transplant is the risk of rejection, not having enough immunosuppression or a risk of developing an infection because you have too much immunosuppression. Again, this will be closely monitored in the post-operative period by our nephrology team and our clinic to make sure we minimize the risk of developing either rejection or infection. There's always a very small chance that the kidney is lost in the post-operative period. This is a very rare event and something that we are very vigilant about making sure does not happen. Our results for our program as well as every other program in the United States are published on the Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients webpage. This can be found by logging into www.srtr.org where you can look up any transplant center programs' results. Here you'll find survival at the one month, one year and three year time intervals for all of our kidney transplant recipients as well as the volume of our program and our wait list size. If you have any questions about how to interpret this data please feel free to reach out to your coordinator or your nephrologist so that we can help explain it to you. You'll also be provided all this information during your visit at our clinic. Please remember that our team is available 24 hours a day, seven days a week to assist you with any needs following your transplant. It is imperative that you stay in communication with us if you develop any signs of a complication or any signs of an infection at any time point following your transplant. For non-urgent questions, we can always be contacted through the MyChart secure email communication tool that you'll be linked to following your transplant. Always remember our phone number is 214-645-1919 and we can be reached at any time of the day for any serious concern. In the event of a serious emergency please remember to call 911 and proceed the closest emergency room and from there please inform that you're a kidney transplant recipient from UT Southwestern and they will contact us and we'll work expeditiously to bring you back to UT Southwestern for further evaluation. Thank you for your time and thank you for choosing UT Southwestern as your provider for kidney transplantation. We look forward to continuing to care for you not only during the transplant procedure but for the years to come. (gentle music)

title: Paired kidney donation: Mayo Clinic Radio
description:
On the Mayo Clinic Radio podcast, Dr. Carrie Schinstock, a Mayo Clinic nephrologist, and Kay Kosberg, a Mayo Clinic nurse who coordinates the paired kidney donation program across Mayo Clinic's Arizona, Florida and Rochester campuses, discuss the paired kidney donation program at Mayo Clinic. 

This interview originally aired Feb. 9, 2019.

Paired donation, also known as "paired exchange," may be an option when a donor and intended recipient have incompatible blood types, or when the recipient has unacceptable antibodies against the donor's tissue antigens. In paired donation, two or more organ recipient pairs trade donors, so that the recipients get organs that are compatible with their blood type. A nondirected living donor also can participate in paired donation to match incompatible pairs. caption_text: Hello. Welcome to the Abdominal Transplant Center at Dell Seton Medical Center at the University of Texas. I'm Katie, the living donor coordinator. In this video, we will go over some educational information on the kidney pair donation, also known as KPD Program for Living Donors. In many instances, recipients have donors that want to donate a kidney on their behalf, but may be incompatible or want to find a better match. With kidney paired exchange, the donor will donate their kidney to another recipient in exchange for a compatible kidney for their recipient, also known as a kidney swap. This could also allow more than one recipient to receive a transplant. The National Kidney Registry, or NKR., facilitates this process. There is a possibility that potential donors will have to wait to find a match, which is often dependent on the recipient's reason for entering kidney paired donation. For example, they are highly sensitized and hard to match, and sometimes even once there is a match, it may take time to schedule the donation due to logistical challenges. There are matching requirements, including: One. Matches are made using a computer program that maximizes the number of matched pairs. Two The computer, finds and displays one solution for each match run. Three. Donors are matched based on donor blood type and antigens compared to candidate blood type and unacceptable antigens. Antigens are proteins that are located on the kidney that can increase someone's risk of rejection. Four. Donor and candidate choices can be used to identify match opportunities such as distance willing to travel but they cannot choose specific individuals or pairs with whom they match. Five. Donors and candidates have the right to decline any match offer. Six. Whether the candidate transplant hospital determines if the matched donor kidney is appropriate for their recipient. And lastly, Seven. The donor and candidate can withdraw from the KPD program at any time for any reason without penalty. The NPR has a voucher program that allows the donor to choose the most convenient time for their donation surgery while providing a voucher to their intended recipient who will be prioritized to receive a transplant if or when they need it. The vouchers include: One. Standard voucher. This is used when a family member or friend is expected to need a kidney transplant within a year, but the donor wants to donate sooner rather than later. Two. Family voucher. This is used when donors do not have someone in immediate need of a transplant. Donors can name up to five family members to receive a voucher. However, once one of the voucher holders redeems the voucher, all other vouchers are void. Three. Swap Saver. This is used when there is a problem with a swap such as the paired recipient being too sick. The parent donor proceeds with surgery to keep the rest of the swap on schedule. The recipient is then prioritized for a transplant and a future swap. And Four. Real time swap failure. This is used when the paired donor donates, but the paired recipient does not get a transplant for whatever reason. The recipient is prioritized for a transplant in a future swap. Remote kidney donation allows someone to donate to a friend or family without requiring a donor to travel to the recipient's transplant center. This lessens the challenges related to traveling for donation and allows the donor to recover at home. Non directed donors are individuals who donate their kidney with no intended recipient. They can participate in the KPD program, donate to a candidate on the deceased donor list, or any other options available in the donor service area. If the donor and recipient are at different transplant centers, the donated kidney is shipped to the recipient center. The kidney is transported by ground transportation or via airplane. Although rare, the following risk may occur. One. Possible delay in the function of the kidney caused by the extra time it takes to transport. And Two. Accidental, complete loss of the donated kidney due to transportation accident or loss between the donor and recipient centers. The NKR uses GPS devices to track all donated kidneys. There are possible adverse events that could occur during KPD donor and recipient surgeries, including but not limited to: One. An event may occur that makes it necessary to stop a donor procedure. In this case, one recipient would not receive a kidney. If a donor or recipient surgery has begun, this surgery will continue even if another surgery in the match must stop. Two. It is possible that impaired recipient will not receive a transplant because of an unexpected issue with their donors kidney found during or after surgery. Three. The donated kidney might not be transplanted or the paired recipient might not receive a transplant due to unexpected events. Four. If the recipient surgery must stop prior to transplantation, that kidney would be made available to another recipient on the deceased donor waiting list. Five. If the donor was to develop chronic kidney disease requiring transplant after donation, the donor receives prioritization on the kidney transplant waiting list for deceased donor organ, NKR. will also provide priority for living donor Kidney transplant. Six. A donor protection program is available to cover complications that are not reimbursable by the recipient's insurance. Seven. Possibility that the paired recipient and the matched recipient might not have equal outcomes. And finally Eight. Possibility the donor's name appears on the matched candidate's insurance estimation of benefits. Those who participate in KPD are not required to sign a formal contract. However, it is encouraged for all who participate to ask questions and discuss all aspects of KPD to make an informed decision. Once the donor recipient are placed in a swap, changing your mind not only affects the pair but the other participants of the swap. Participants have the right to withdraw from the KPD program at any time, for any reason, and without penalty. There are no binding contracts. Strict privacy, confidentiality and anonymity will be given to donors and recipients during the evaluation, transplantation and post operative process. However, participants in the KPD must agree to allow our center to share your protected health information with the other transplant hospitals participating within the KPD program. Limited information including transmissible diseases, cancer and other results that may affect the health of the recipient will be shared with both the donor and the recipient. Information will also be shared with local, state and federal agencies as required by law. After both surgeries are completed, donors may have the opportunity to communicate with the recipient they donated to. Both parties must agree prior to any communication taking place. Initial communication should be facilitated by the transplant coordinator or social worker responsible for the swap. If a kidney donor experiences complications related to the surgery, medical costs should be paid by the recipient's insurance. Sometimes insurance companies limit the coverage. The donor protection program through the and NKR eliminates this risk in partnership with our program. We would pay for medical cost of uncovered complications. As a donor shield program center, we offer protections to donors who donate through an NKR exchange. All donors who donate at a donor shield center will receive the following protections. One. Lost wage reimbursement for up to six weeks with a max $2,000 per week reimbursement after donation. Two. Travel, lodging and mileage reimbursement up to $5,000 for donors and their support person or travel companion. Three. Access to reasonably priced Life Insurance through National Kidney Registry. Four. Legal Support. Five. Coverage for uncovered donor complication costs. And finally, Six. Lost wage and travel reimbursement for subsequent donor complications. Thank you for choosing Dell Seton Medical Center at the University of Texas at Austin and becoming a living kidney donor. Remember, we are here to support you during your living donor journey. Please contact your living donor coordinator with any questions.

Transplant surgeon Dr. Andrew Cameron answers common questions about liver disease and transplant options. To learn more visit hopkinsmedicine.org/transplant

(light music) >> Liver transplant is
considered when a patient has end stage liver disease or cirrhosis. Cirrhosis in the United
States is most commonly caused by hepatitis C virus
infection or alcohol use, but there are other conditions that could also cause cirrhosis; auto-immune conditions like
primary sclerosing cholangitis or primary biliary cirrhosis. There are even conditions
that effect little kids like biliary atresia that can cause the need for a liver transplant. (light music) Unfortunately when a patient
becomes sick with a bad liver there aren't great medical options, there aren't great medicines, and there certainly is
no dialysis for the liver so a liver transplant becomes
the only and best option. In terms of liver transplant, there are basically two options. The first is to get a liver
transplant from a person who has passed away and
decided to donate their organs. That's a whole liver
from a deceased owner. The other option is to
get half of a liver, a partial liver transplant,
from a living donor. (light music) We know that a living
donor partial transplant has excellent results equal
to that for a whole graft. The advantage would be
that you don't have to wait for your liver transplant
if you have a living donor. There are 7,000 Americans on the liver transplant wait list now and the wait can be years and that can be very
difficult for sick patients. If you're lucky enough to have
an appropriate living donor, you don't have to wait on the list. (light music) The most exciting development
over the last couple of years in liver transplant is the arrival of powerful new anti-hep C meds. Hepatitis C used to be a very
difficult disease to treat. The medicines weren't very good
and they were pretty toxic. Maybe two years ago we have
discovered new anti-virals. They are pills that are taken
once a day for 12 weeks. They cure hepatitis C 98% of the time and they are very well tolerated. This has entirely changed the game for liver transplantation for hepatitis C. Now many patients have had hepatitis C often for 20 years without knowing it, so clearing the virus, while
it's wonderful, good news, may not prevent their need
for a liver transplant, but if they get a liver
transplant and take these meds, hepatitis C will not come
back after a liver transplant and that's a huge improvement
in terms of how the liver will work and how long it will last. (light music) The biggest risk is not
getting your liver transplant. We know that it is incredibly difficult for patients on the wait list. We know with mathematical certainty that if they need a liver transplant and they don't get one
they will die waiting. Liver transplant itself
certainly has it's own risks, but for example, the one year survival after liver transplant is over 90%, so if you get a liver transplant
the odds are very much in your favor that a year later and far beyond you'll be alive and well. Specifically we always
worry about infection after a liver transplant
because you have to take meds so that you don't reject your new liver, those cause immunosuppression. We worry about bleeding
during a liver transplant, but for the most part,
complications are very well handled and long term success is the
rule after a liver transplant. (light music) Patients with liver
disease are very complex and they benefit from a team approach. They don't need just a surgeon, they need an entire team, a team with a hepatologist, a dietician, a pharmacist, a social
worker, a psychologist. We know that when patients have an entire team results are better. Our goal is not just to
perform a liver transplant, it's to restore sick patient to their normal state of
health and well-being. To make sure that the
patient really thrives we know that we do best with
a multi-disciplinary approach. (light music)

pancreatitis. Endoscopic therapy is most commonly
offered to those patients who have a dilated
pancreatic duct. These patients can undergo an endoscopic

pancreatic ducts stents. [MUSIC] For those patients with small duct disease

and total pancreatectomy. And for patients with large duct disease,
they can be offered procedures such as the Frey and

approach to evaluating and managing patients with
chronic pancreatitis. We are constantly looking for new medical,
endoscopic and surgical therapies for treating the
very difficult patients. There have been some developments in the field of endoscopic ultrasound with celiac
plexus blockade. This procedure can be used to help alleviate the pain associated with chronic
pancreatitis. At least in the short term as more long
term options are pursued. The the greatest option that has emerged
over the years for the surgical treatment of chronic pancreatitis is total pancreatectomy with or without islet cell

>> As we begin it is important to talk
about how lung transplantation differs from other solid organ transplants. The heart, liver and kidneys are all
contained completely inside the body. Lungs are large solid organs
that while contained in the chest are constantly
exposed to the external environment. Everything we inhale goes through the lungs. These are like big filters. There are a lot of cells within the lungs
that protect us from getting infections. You can inhale any type of virus, bacteria
or fungi through the lungs as well. After transplantation you will be on many
medications that suppress your immune system so your body can accept the
new lungs and not reject them. Because of the constant exposure to the
external environment we have more problems with infections and organ rejection with
lung transplantation than with other organs. That in combination with the
fact that there are just not that many donor lungs available has made
identifying eligible transplant candidates extremely important. Consequently our medical transplant evaluation
will probably be the most thorough exam you've ever had. Your medical evaluation will be performed
by one of our transplant pulmonologists. During this exam your pulmonologist
assesses the extent of your lung disease and your medical suitability for
transplantation and discusses the significance of transplantation including
the risks and complications. Your pulmonologist also manages transplant
related medical needs prior to transplantation, participates in care during the
transplant hospital admission, monitors immunosuppressive medications and manages your medical care following
lung transplantation after discharge. To start this exam you will
have a lot of blood drawn. Many tests are run so your pulmonologist
can get a picture of your overall health. Your blood will also be tested
for the presence of nicotine, chronic substance use, alcohol
and illicit drug use. If you were a smoker you have to be smoke-free for at least six months prior
to your evaluation. This includes any nicotine containing
products such as gum or patches. If you continue to smoke, you will
not be a candidate for transplant. Any evidence of chronic substance
use, heavy alcohol use or illicit drug use makes you
ineligible for a transplant evaluation. You must cease using these substances for
at least six months prior to evaluation. Your weight and nutritional
status are also important factors when we're evaluating you for transplant. If you are too skinny you
may be malnourished with all of your calories going towards
helping you breathe. Underwent patients do not do
well after transplant surgery. On the other hand, obese patients tend
not to do well after surgery either. To frame this discussion about your weight,
your pulmonologist will use the body mass index and discuss the specifics with you. You will be required to participate
in an exercise program. Lung transplantation is a big operation. You need to be in the best physical shape
possible to prepare for this surgery. Exercise will help condition you for surgery. You will also be asked to
perform a six minute hall walk. During this time you must be
able to walk at least 450 feet. As we have said before, lung
transplantation is a big surgery. You must be strong enough going into the
surgery to be able to recover successfully. If you are already in a wheelchair and
cannot walk because of shortness of breath, you may be too weak to be a candidate. Other tests you will need include
a cotinine test, chest x-ray, 24-hour pH probe and an arterial blood gas. Since you'll be on corticosteroids after
transplant you'll need a bone densitometry test. Corticosteroids can break down your
bones over time and we have to treat that effectively to prevent any complications. Certain tests like colonoscopy,
mammograms, Pap smear and rectal and prostate exams may be handled
by your primary care physician. Your regular physician is also instrumental
in managing other maintenance issues like immunizations for hepatitis A and
B as well as testing for tuberculosis. You will need to get medical
clearance from your dentist as well. Let's look at some reasons you may not
be eligible for lung transplantation. Many of the anti-rejection medicines we use
actually speed up the growth of cancer cells. If you have a history of

consider you for lung transplantation. The only exception to the five

program at the University of Michigan. There are other conditions that may
make you ineligible for lung transplant. If you are chronically ventilator
dependant, have active or current antibiotic resistant infections,
suffer from an incapacitating mental illness, have systemic disorders such as connective
tissue diseases, demyelization disorders or are nursing home dependant we cannot
consider you for transplantation.

placement on the waiting list. With the lung allocation score, whoever's
the sickest will go to the top of the list. When lungs become available, a suitable

title: How do I qualify for a kidney transplant?
description:
Presented by Dr. Melissa Isbell, nephrologist with Renal Associates and a former Chief of Staff at Methodist Specialty and Transplant Hospital.
"To receive a kidney transplant there are several requirements that need to be met. And these are requirements that are established nationally and by our program. At the Texas Transplant Institute, we help patients through every step of the process to ensure they are a good candidate for kidney transplantation and have great results." Click the video to learn more.
caption_text:
(What does it take to qualify for a kidney transplant?) - To receive a kidney transplant, there are several requirements
that need to be met. And these are requirements that
are established nationally, and also by our program. Generally, you need to
have kidney function that's poor enough to
require a transplant, which means a GFR, or glomerular filtration
rate, less than 20. Generally we'd like your
age to be less than 70, at times we will adjust this,
but generally less than 70. We would like you not to smoke. We would like you not to use
any illegal drugs whatsoever. You should have good
health maintenance updates, you should have your teeth evaluated on a regular basis and
have good dentition. If you're over 50, you
should have a colonoscopy. If you have high blood pressure, diabetes, you will need to have
cardiac testing performed. And if you're a woman, you will need a mammogram or a PAP smear. If you're a man, you
will need to have a PSA and a digital rectal examination. If you've had active
cardiac disease in the past, you will need to have
cardiac studies performed and be cleared by your cardiologist. If you've been on dialysis
for a period of time, you may require imaging
studies of your kidneys, either an ultrasound or a CAT scan. You need to have no evidence of any active liver disease, such as cirrhosis. And you need to have a
good social circumstance and supportive family when you
go home after the transplant. It's also important that you have a good, reasonable financial plan
following the transplant, so that you are able to pay for
your medications afterwards, and keep your follow-up,
and maintain this kidney that was a gift of life to you. (For additional information: 1-800-888-0402)

caption_text: hello i'm dr kevin thomas a cardiac electrophysiologist with the norton heart and vascular institute an implantable cardioverter defibrillator commonly known as an icd is a device designed to administer life-saving therapy in the event of a cardiac arrest your doctor may recommend this procedure if you have previously experienced or are at increased risk for life-threatening abnormal heart rhythms called ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation these life-threatening rhythms can cause sudden cardiac arrest which can lead to death if not immediately treated the icd monitors your heart rhythm 24 hours per day and when the icd senses a dangerous life-threatening heart rhythm it will send an electrical pulse to your heart to reset its normal rhythm and allow your heart to resume pumping blood through your body this is known as defibrillation the icd is composed of a generator which is the small lightweight metal case that contains the battery and circuitry and leads which are insulated flexible wires that are placed in the heart and attached to the generator an icd may have one two or three leads depending on each patient's specific condition the icd implantation procedure takes between one to two hours and is performed in the electrophysiology laboratory of the hospital where you'll be placed on an x-ray table you may be given medications intravenously to sedate you or make you sleepy these medications help reduce your anxiety and relieve discomfort your chest area will be cleaned with antiseptic and sterile drapes will be placed to cover your body a local anesthetic will be administered with a tiny needle to numb the area where the incision will be made you will feel a pin prick and possibly a stinging sensation for a few seconds a small incision approximately three to four inches long will then be made in the upper chest area just below your collarbone and a small pouch or pocket will be created under the skin where the generator will be placed the lead or leads will then be inserted into a vein in the upper chest and advance to the heart under x-ray guidance once the lead or leads are in the proper position within the heart they will be tested to make sure they sense the heart signals correctly they will then be connected to the generator and the generator and leads will be placed in the pocket the incision will then be closed and covered with addressing following the procedure you will be moved to a recovery area to rest quietly for several hours your heartbeat and blood pressure will be monitored continuously to check for complications often patients are able to go home the same day but your physician may elect to keep you overnight for monitoring and pain control upon discharge you will get information about how to care for yourself after the procedure including medication changes wound care activity guidelines device care and maintenance and a follow-up schedule be sure to review pre and post documents on what to do before and after the procedure as always if you have questions please reach out to your doctor's office thank you for choosing norton heart and vascular - Welcome to Henry Ford Health Transplant and thank you for
choosing our team to care for your kidney transplant needs. I am Dean Kim, surgical director of the Kidney and Pancreas
Transplant Program. Please write down any
questions you may think of during this video. We are happy to answer
any of your questions or discuss any topics further. The listing process sorts
through your medical problems to assure that kidney
transplant will benefit you. Some medical history will be gathered when you schedule your first appointment. At your appointment you'll learn more about transplant process
from a nurse coordinator. Next step is to meet with
the clinical team members including a transplant nephrologist a social worker, a transplant surgeon, and a dietician if indicated. Your transplant nurse will give you a list of required tests and appointments. You'll need to work with your transplant nurse
to complete these tests and have the results reviewed. Once all of your results are in order your case will be discussed at our selection meeting
where a decision will be made about your listing for transplant. Your nurse coordinator will
discuss this decision with you. If listed, you will be
seen annually by our team. Once listed you are eligible
for kidney transplant from either a living or a deceased donor. Living donor kidney is
usually from a friend, a family member or anyone
who is willing to donate and is found to be
healthy enough to donate. Your nurse coordinator can provide you with information on the website where living donors can
sign up and be tested. There are several benefits for living donor kidney transplants. The living donor kidney is usually of good quality and lasts longer. A living donor kidney lasts
on average 12 to 15 years whereas a kidney from
a deceased donor lasts, on average, eight to 10 years. Living donor kidney
transplants can happen earlier in the process rather than waiting years on dialysis and it's associated with fewer complications
around the time of surgery. Living donor surgery is
scheduled at an agreed upon time that's best for
the donor and recipient. While matched recipients may need less anti-rejection medicine, living donation also minimizes the chances of delayed function of
the transplanted kidney. Finally, some living donor
kidney transplants can be done with a robot, reducing the size and complications of the incision. A kidney's quality can be estimated by the kidney donor profile index or KDPI. The KDPI can be used to estimate how long a transplanted kidney will last. The lower the KDPI the longer the kidney is expected to last. Kidneys with low KDPI
are usually offered first to children and young adults on the list. Higher KDPI kidneys, especially
those with KDPI over 85, are usually offered to older recipients or those with diseases like diabetes, which make dialysis more
difficult to tolerate long term. For recipients who are waiting for deceased donor transplant you should see the kidney
transplant team once yearly or if you're older than the
age of 70 years, twice yearly. This is important to update
your social support, insurance, medical tests, medications,
and review new issues. When we call you about a
kidney transplant offer we will ask a series of questions to see if anything has changed since the last time you
were seen in our clinic. We will discuss if there is
anything that you should know about the kidney prior
to agreeing to proceed. All kidneys accepted for transplant can carry a risk of infection. This infection could be bacterial, viral, or less commonly from yeast or fungus. For example, if a donor is found to have a bacterial
infection prior to donation, we may consult with our
infectious disease colleagues and decide to accept the kidney for you, despite the infection
that is already present. We may choose to continue
antibiotic therapy in you for a certain time. All kidneys are tested for viruses such as COVID-19, hepatitis and HIV. One way to protect against
this infection is to be vaccinated for viruses
prior to transplant. However, sometimes,
despite our best testing of the donor kidney,
infection can sneak through. For example, HIV or
hepatitis can be transmitted with the organ about one in 7,000 cases. The risk is very low but present. If a kidney donor is involved in behavior that would put them at a higher risk for transmitting a virus, for example, jail time
or intravenous drug use, the risk of disease transmission for HIV or hepatitis would be between
one in 100 to one in 4,000. You'll be told if your donor
falls into this category and you'll have the opportunity
to accept this kidney or pass on this kidney. Regardless, all kidney
transplant recipients are tested for HIV and hepatitis during the first year after transplant. You may opt to receive
a kidney from a donor that has tested positive
to have hepatitis C. The benefit is that
you may be transplanted and off dialysis sooner. Hepatitis C is a virus that
survives in your liver. Successful treatment for
hepatitis C is available. If you choose to receive a kidney from a donor with hepatitis C you will need to take extra
medicines by mouth for 12 weeks. The rate of cure of hepatitis C with treatment is 95 to 100%. Delayed graft function
occurs when the kidney is not working well enough to keep the recipient off dialysis. The transplanted kidney has
been through a lot of stress and it may take a few days to a few weeks for the kidney to regain
its ability to filter and make urine. While the kidney is slow to function, you may need to be
supported with hemodialysis. If needed, dialysis can be continued in your regular center
or sometimes at home if that is where you were
getting dialysis prior. If you were on peritonealdialysis
prior to transplant you will need to be
switched to hemodialysis. Delayed graft function occurs
after transplant in 25 to 50% of patients and a very small
number of kidneys never work. This is called primary non-function and occurs only about
one to 2% of the time. The important thing to remember is that delayed graft function is common and primary non-function is rare. Be patient, the vast majority of kidneys recover
despite delayed function. - Hi, I'm Jason Denny. I'm the director of the
Center for Living Donation. I'm also the surgical director of the Living Donor
Kidney Transplant Program at Henry Ford Health. When you're called in for a
kidney transplant, you will go to the H6 floor and be
tested for COVID-19. If the COVID- 19 testing is negative you will proceed to the
preoperative area where you will meet your surgeon
and anesthesia teams. There you'll complete your
pre-transplant testing. If you need dialysis that can
be done prior to transplant. The surgical team will
check the transplant kidney in the operating room. If it looks okay and you
look okay, you will proceed to the operating room
for four to six hours. You'll be given general anesthesia. The typical kidney transplant incision is near the right lower abdomen. During the operation, your
native kidneys are not removed. A third or fourth kidney will be placed in the front of the stomach,
usually on the right side. The native kidneys will
continue to atrophy or shrink and get smaller over time. The surgeon will create an incision and find the blood vessels that run to and from your leg as well as a bladder. The surgeon will implant the kidney. The kidney transplant can also be done with the assistance of
a robot, which results in smaller wounds and
reduced wound complications. There are three main connections made during the transplant of the kidney. The first and second
surgical connections are between the transplant
renal vein and artery, and the iliac vein and artery. This returns blood flow
to the transplant kidney. The ureter is a tube that carries
the urine from the kidney. A third surgical connection is made between the transplant
ureter and your bladder to drain any urine that
the kidney produces. A drain is placed near the
kidney to drain any fluids that collect around the kidney. We will be watching the amount and character of the drainage. We can remove the drain once we are happy with the quality and the amount is less than
100 milliliters in 24 hours. A stitch is placed over
the drain site at the time of removal to prevent the
drain site from leaking after the drain is removed. Sometimes it is necessary to
send you home with your drain. In this case, you will be
taught how to care for the drain and empty and record its output at home. If you are sent home with the drain you will need to keep
the site clean and dry. Often a stent is inserted between the ureter and the bladder. This stays for about three weeks while the surgical connection between the ureter and the bladder heals. A drain is left inside at
the time of the surgery near this connection. The drain can help remove any excess fluid from the area around the
new kidney transplant. Output from the drain
can also help identify if there is a leak. A complication where the urine is leaking through the connection. This occurs in approximately
one to 3% of patients. The stent is removed by
cystoscopy, an outpatient procedure which does not
require general anesthesia. - Hi, I'm Lauren Malinzak, a kidney and pancreas transplant surgeon, the director of H6 where you will stay as a transplant patient at Henry Ford. The Henry Ford transplant team consists of eight transplant surgeons Dr. Kim, Dr. Denny and I do
most of the kidney transplants. After surgery most patients go to H6, the transplant surgery floor. The team there is very familiar with taking care of transplant patients. By day one, you'll be out
of bed at least to a chair. Your team will assess the
function of the kidney transplant and need for dialysis every day. You may need an ultrasound. You will be able to drink
if you're not nauseated. By day two you'll be out of bed walking, back to eating and drinking
as you tolerate it. You and your support will learn about your medications for home. By day three, your
catheter will be removed. After you can urinate on your own your drain will be removed. Discharge plans will be finalized. While you're in the hospital, the clinical team will be
watching for complications. These complications can be categorized as bleeding, thrombosis,
infection fluid collections or problems with the ureter or bladder. In addition to getting
infection from the kidney, patients can acquire
infections in the hospital such as pneumonia, blood or wound infections. Bleeding complications
can include bleeding from or around the kidney transplant. Blood transfusion is needed
in about 20% of patients who undergo a kidney transplant. More so if you're starting the surgery with a low blood count. About two to 4% of patients will return to the operating room for
bleeding complications. Those numbers can double if you need blood thinners
such as warfarin or Plavix. We do not transplant
deceased donor kidneys into patients taking
medications such as Eliquis. Thrombosis is when blood clots. Blood can clot in or
around the kidney leading to loss of the kidney transplant
in up to 4% of patients. If this occurs, the kidney
would need to be removed and you would return to dialysis. You can also get blood clots in veins such as your legs or pelvis or in your lungs. This kind of blood clot would need to be treated with blood thinners. The best way to prevent
blood clots in your legs is to wear the sequential
compression devices while you are in bed. Ambulate as soon as possible
and frequently after surgery and you'll be given a
blood thinner, heparin, under your skin two to three times a day while in the hospital. We'll be watching for
symptoms of infection daily. If you are heavier or diabetic, you'll be at higher risk for wound infections. Sometimes you may be asked to lose weight or get better control of your blood sugar prior to transplant to reduce this risk. Ureter complications can
include leaking at the site of the connection or the
connection can scar down and become too tight for
urine to pass through. This is known as stenosis. Bladder complications can occur
when you have difficulties with urination after transplant. A variety of issues can
occur such as bladder spasms, which can be painful or irritating. Frequent urination, urinary incontinence, urinary retention, which
may require catheterization, or the urine stream may be
blocked by a large prostate. Most but not all urinary
and bladder complications can be managed with treatment that doesn't require repeat operation. Hernias can occur after
open kidney transplant due to the location of the
incision, being overweight, or requiring immunosuppression. To prevent this you may
be required to lose weight prior to surgery, be given an abdominal binder
to wear to reduce strain on the wound and you'll not be able to
do any strenuous activity or lifting anything greater than 10 pounds for two to three months after transplant. At the end of one year,
our expected patient and graft survival is
approximately 95 to 97%. At the time of transplant you will start anti-rejection medications through an IV in the operating room. You'll need to take
anti-rejection medications by mouth twice daily for as
long as you have the transplant. You'll start with larger doses
and these doses will taper down over the first three to
six months after transplant. These medications have side effects. Most commonly, they
cause GI upset, diarrhea, skin and hair changes. One of these medications we
give you is called tacrolimus. This medication must be
kept within a certain range. If it is too low, you'll get rejection and if the dose is too
high, certain side effects like headaches, shaking,
and even seizures can occur. Overall, these medications
reduce your body's ability to fight infection and cancer. It's very important to learn from patients already
living with transplant how to live safely in your community. After transplant, you'll
need your support people. They will help you with everything from your discharge
instructions, medications, transportation, to attending
your clinic visits with you. You won't be able to lift
anything heavier than 10 pounds so you'll need help with
laundry, dishes, cooking, and other daily activities. You'll be able to shower but no baths, hot tubs or swimming pools
are allowed after transplant. You'll be able to take a bath once your incision is completely healed. You'll be attending
clinic about twice weekly for the first couple
months after transplant. When things become more stable you'll see us less and less. Plan to take about three

caption_text: Hi, my name is Sarah Householder and I'm going to talk to you about how to take care of someone in your life who needs a liver transplant. As patients get closer to transplant, they become more and more reliant on their support networks and support people. Yet, most people step into this role from a place of love, not from experience. We created this guide as a way to help you understand how you can help take care of your loved one who needs a liver transplant. The biggest question to start with is how does someone get a liver transplant? Whenever someone's liver is getting worse, they'll be referred to a transplant center by their GI doctor or hepatologist. After the initial evaluation, the patient and their support person will receive an education. And the patient will undergo an evaluation that'll include doctor's visits, blood tests, imaging, and a social work evaluation to make sure that they'll be successful after an intensive surgery. After the evaluation is done, they'll be reviewed by a transplant board and if approved, listed for transplant. This process can take weeks to months, all while having a sick liver. As a result, most patients experience worse health during this period and may need to be hospitalized once or several times. They will need to take medications and for some patients have procedures to help stabilize their liver. Most patients during this period experience sadness, stress, and anxiety. Caretakers play a large role during this process, and you are crucial to a patient's ability to be successful. We have some strategies that will help you help your loved one. First, get organized. Keep track of appointments, medications, important dates. Try and learn everything you can about the liver, the transplant process, and their specific disease. Communicate often with the transplant team and try and attend appointments as often as you can so you can hear all the information. At home, you can help the patient follow a high protein, low salt diet, keep up their strength for surgery, and completely avoid alcohol during the transplant evaluation process. You can also help them keep track of their medications, and pay attention to any side effects. Make sure you wash all fruits and vegetables carefully and wash your hands often to avoid getting infections. And finally, try and be patient with your loved one as during this time they may experience mood swings, frustration, and sadness. This may be related to something called hpatic encphylopathy or HE. H is caused by a buildup of ammonia in the blood which is normally cleared by the liver. Common symptoms include forgetfulness, sleep changes, disorientation, and personality and behavior changes. If you notice any symptoms of H, it's important to let your transplant center know right away. Finally, one of the most important things that you can do is remember to take care of yourself. The road to transplant can be very long and most caregivers experience something called burnout or exhaustion from stress. The best way we have to prevent burnout is instead of relying all on one person, try and build a network of support of people who can share responsibility. Try and take breaks for yourself and remember to take care of your own health. In the midst of all of this, try and protect your relationship to the patient before you became a caregiver and find moments for that. And lastly, build community. Ask your transplant center about networks that exist both locally and nationally to help caregivers find other people going through similar processes. For many, this may be one of the most difficult periods in life. Yet, we want you to remember that you are not alone and that on your care team, there are a lot of providers who care about their patient and want to make sure that they are successful. Thank you.

(dramatic music) >> Alcoholic hepatitis is
a serious medical condition in which a patient may experience rapid, acute liver failure in response to recent intake of alcohol. It's really a spectrum of diseases. It can be mild, but in some scenarios, it can be life-threatening. (dramatic music) Well unfortunately, the treatment
options are very limited. We give patients IV steroids, and some of them respond and improve. Unfortunately, a large
percentage of patients with alcoholic hepatitis do
not improve with steroids, and we can only provide

severe alcoholic hepatitis, and that's the possibility of

been considered eligible for a liver transplant, because of the six-month waiting period. There is a rule in the United States that you cannot have a liver transplant if you've not been sober for six months. That rule is now being challenged. (dramatic music) In 2011, there was a very
important paper published in the New England Journal of Medicine, in which 27 patients that had
severe alcoholic hepatitis underwent early liver transplant with a waiver of the
six-month waiting period. We have run a pilot
program at Johns Hopkins, in which we have also
transplanted patients without a six-month waiting period. We found that in the 46 patients that were critically ill with

title: Living Organ Donation at UVA Health
description:
#livingdonor
Living organ donors can save lives by donating an organ while they're still alive. Living organ donation is an option for kidney and liver transplants only. Nurse practitioner Anita Sites explains the process of becoming a living donor. 
Find out more at: https://uvahealth.com/services/transplant/living-donations
Transcript:
I'm Anita Sites. I'm a nurse practitioner. And my primary role is working with our living donor population. There's close to 20,000 people waiting for liver transplants in the United States, and there are just not enough deceased donor organs to supply all those people in need. Donors are, of course, the heroes of transplant, but living donors are especially special. They are giving of themselves in the most ultimate way, for no benefit for themselves. So the evaluation process is a really thorough one. You know it's not an overnight process. And we have to make sure that at height of our priority list is the donor’s safety and well-being. It's a commitment to the process. It's also a commitment to the recovery. And then we follow them for at least two years. So it's a commitment to that process as well. Donors are heroes. They don't always want to be recognized as heroes, but they are heroes. And that's how we get to come to work every day and take care of them and to transport people and to save their lives. Multidisciplinary team members
meet with each potential donor. There's a ton of blood work that we do to evaluate them, and then we really do extensive imaging of their abdomen. We do a CT scan, we do an MRI. So it's really a head to toe very thorough evaluation to make sure that no stone is unturned and that any risk that we find along the way that we're able to eliminate those risks, to really minimize the potential for negative outcomes for the donor or for complications. And then once a donor is approved for surgery, we really work with them to see what would work best in terms of their schedule and their life to be able to do this.

selection criteria are specific to Mass General though many of them are used at transplant centers across the country all living donors must be at least 18 years old and any non-directive donors or donors who do not have a specific kidney recipient in mind must be at least 25 years old all donors must be donating voluntarily and not be feeling pressured or coerced into their decision donors should be in good overall physical and mental health including being free from diabetes which is the leading cause of kidney disease having a BMI or body mass index of 35 or less at the time of evaluation and ideally a BMI of 32 or less by the time of donation surgery having no active drug or alcohol abuse or no significant history of drug or alcohol abuse having no significant medical conditions such as heart lung or liver diseases bleeding or clotting disorders recent cancer those skin cancers other than melanoma are usually acceptable but most other types of cancer will require years of remission being free from HIV active hepatitis B and C or other infections or behaviors that increase the risk of developing these infections having no significant psychiatric conditions requiring significant treatment or at higher risk of recurrence having either current or a history of kidney stones or high blood pressure will require additional testing to determine whether the donor is acceptable or ruled out being willing to stop all forms of smoking for at least eight weeks prior to donation surgery and stop any oral contraceptive pills and usually hormone replacement therapy for four weeks prior to and after donation surgery for direct donation where the donor donates their kidney directly to their intended recipient the first item we consider is blood type there are four blood types o a B and a B donors who are blood type O are considered the universal donor and can donate to a recipient with any blood type donors with blood type A can donate to recipients with blood type A or a B donors with blood type E can donate to recipients with blood types B or AV donors with web type a B can only donate to recipients who also have blood type a B most of the time when people find out their blood type they also get a positive or negative at the end which is the Rh type this marker is found on red blood cells but not on kidney cells for this reason the RH type does not matter for kidney donation the second major item we consider when determining if a potential donor is compatible with their intended recipient is to see if the recipient has HLA antibodies against the donor HLA stands for human leukocyte antigens and these are the markers on the outside of everyone's cells that tell the body which cells are their own and shouldn't be attacked versus foreign cells like a bacteria or virus that should be attacked many recipients do not have any HLA antibodies the usual way that patients develop these antibodies are through prior transplants pregnancies blood transfusions or on very rare occasions infections there are a few tests that are performed to determine HLA compatibility for the recipient the testing involves seeing if the recipient has antibodies against any HLA antigen the donor is tested to see what HLA antigens they have on their cells the tissue typing lab can then compare the results to see if the recipient has antibodies specific to the donors antigens if it appears that the recipient does have these donors specific antibodies a cross-match bait may be performed where the recipient and donor blood samples are mixed to see if the recipient serum destroys the donor cells if the cross match is positive meaning that the cells are destroyed the donor would not be able to donate directly to their recipient as the recipient will reject the donors kidney even if the cross match is initially negative or therapy and does not have any antibodies a cross match will be performed 1 to 2 weeks prior to the donation and transplant surgery date just to minimize the chance that there are any newly developed antibodies that could cause immediate rejection of the donor kidney if the recipient and donor are found to be incompatible either due to blood type or donors specific antibody there are two options available the first option is for the donor and recipient to be entered into the kidney paired donation or KPD program in this situation the donor would donate to a compatible recipient and the recipient at Mass General would receive a kidney from a compatible live donor as part of a swap the picture here illustrates the simplest form of pair exchange where pair 1 and pair 2 are incompatible so donor 1 donates to recipient 2 and donor 2 donates to recipient 1 this simple swap is relatively rare and more often swaps involve multiple pairs of donors and recipients there is a separate video available that provides more information about the KTV process the second option for incompatible pairs is desensitization the goal of desensitization is to remove donor specific antibodies from the recipients blood however the process is not possible for some recipients involves giving the Hello, on behalf of the Froedtert & the   Medical College of Wisconsin Kidney and Pancreas 
Transplant Program, I would like to congratulate   you on your recent transplant. You will be 
discharged home from the hospital soon. We want   to ensure a smooth transition from the hospital to 
your home. Before you go, there are a few things   we want you to know. Before we get started, you 
will receive all of the information I am about to   share with you in writing if you haven't already. 
First, you must take all of your medications as   prescribed. If you miss a dose, call your 
transplant coordinator right away. Second,   your anti-rejection medicines will be taken 
at the same time in the morning and evening,   12 hours apart. On lab days, you will need to 
have your blood drawn at the time you would   normally take your morning medications. You must 
wait until after after your blood is drawn to take   your medications. This is extremely important. 
If you accidentally take your medications before   your blood is drawn, please let your transplant 
coordinator know. Having a support person is   critical to success after transplant. You will 
need your support person to stay with you for a   minimum of 7 days. They should help you with your 
medications, meal preparation, lifting, household   chores and transportation. It is so important that 
they come with you to your clinic appointments so   that they know how to help you through your 
recovery. You should drink eight glasses of   water per day to stay hydrated. This is a big 
change from before transplant where you had a   fluid restriction. It can sometimes be a difficult 
adjustment. If you have a blood pressure cuff,   thermometer and scale, you should be taking these 
readings every morning and writing the results in   your transplant booklet. This booklet should be 
brought to the clinic with you and shared with   your transplant team. You will be given a urine 
collection container before discharge. There are   markings on each container that will allow you 
to measure the amount of urine you make. Please   record the amount in your transplant booklet. If 
you are diabetic or are new to needing insulin,   you will need to check your blood sugars before 
each meal and before bedtime. Your results must   be written down in your transplant booklet. Please 
know that your transplant team does not manage   your blood sugars or insulin. Your inpatient 
care team will let you know who to follow up   with after you leave the hospital. If you are 
going home with a drain, you will likely need   to empty it several times per day. It is okay to 
empty it when it is close to being full. Please   empty the drainage in the container provided 
to you and record the amount in your transplant   booklet. Make sure the bulb is squeezed and held 
while putting the cap back on to ensure proper   suction. You may then dump the drainage from 
the measuring container into the toilet. There   may be times when you will need to contact your 
transplant team no matter what time of day it is -   if you are experiencing a fever of 100.5 degrees 
or higher; if you notice a decrease in your urine   output, urgency or pain with urination; if you are 
unable to keep your medications or fluids down;   if you have any unexplained abdominal pain or pain 
over the transplant site; if you have weight gain   of 3 pounds in 24 hours or 5 pounds in 1 week; 
and finally, if you have redness, swelling,   pus or an open area at your transplant site. We 
want you to feel confident as you return home   following your transplant. Your transplant 
team is here to help you navigate life as a   transplant patient. Receiving a transplant does 
not mean your disease is cured. You are still a   patient with chronic health conditions that need 
to be managed. There will still be ups and downs,   and we are here to see you through them. 
Following the instructions provided to you   by your transplant team will allow you to 
maintain good health and continually care   for this gift of life. If you experience 
any of the issues discussed in this video,   please contact your transplant team. To reach 
your transplant coordinator Monday through   Friday from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., please 
call 414-805-3100. For any concerns after   hours or on the weekends or holidays, please 
call our Access Center at 414-805-4700. Make   sure to inform them that you are a transplant 
patient and need to speak with a member of   your transplant team. Thank you for choosing 
Froedtert & the Medical College of Wisconsin.

title: Mayo Clinic Minute: Living donor organ transplants
description:
If you’re among the 54 percent of American adults who’ve registered to be an organ donor, it’s encouraging to know your decision could end up saving the lives of up to eight people. A living donor transplant, naturally, is handled differently and often comes about when a friend or family member has a dire need.

Although, in the case of kidney transplants, altruistic, or good Samaritan, donations have been on the rise. 

"Some people just come forward as a potential donor wanting to help a needy patient that’s on the waiting list," says Dr. Charles Rosen, director of Mayo Clinic's Transplant Center. "Another thing that happens is a donor and recipient pair come forward, where it’s not a match for one reason or another, and they may exchange kidneys with another donor-recipient pair."

In April, which is National Donate Life Month, Dennis Douda shares more of Dr. Rosen's thoughts.

More health and medical news on the Mayo Clinic News Network http://newsnetwork.mayoclinic.org/

title: The organ transplant journey: how the organ donation process works
description:
Organ donation and transplantation is a complex process, requiring the expertise and collaboration of thousands across the country every day. This intricate journey begins with one person – the organ donor. Join UNOS as we explore this lifesaving system from the perspective of the generous organ donor, their willing family and the organ procurement organization on the ground.

For more information, visit: https://unos.org/transplant/deceased-donation/

To register to become an organ donor, visit: https://www.registerme.org/
caption_text:
Organ donation
and transplantation is a complex process requiring the expertise and collaboration of thousands every day. The intricate journey begins with the generosity of one person: the organ donor. Organ donors are hospitalized
patients on ventilators whose brains or hearts
have stopped functioning often due to a tragic injury, but whose organs are still viable. After exhausting all means
to save the patient's life, the hospital contacts their organ procurement
organization or OPO. OPO staff are trained to
counsel patients' families at the worst moment of their lives. If the patient is a
registered organ donor, the OPO helps the family
understand the process they're about to go through. If the patient is not registered, the OPO offers the family
the option to donate. This is a transformative decision. A single donor can save up to eight lives. Eye and tissue donors can heal even more. Once authorization is obtained, the OPO begins working to match the organ with a critically ill patient. Currently more than 100,000 patients are on the national waiting list, maintained by the United Network
for Organ Sharing or UNOS. OPO staff first determine if the donor's organs are
viable for transplant, and then enters their medical information into the UNOS database, which generates a list of best matches based on a variety of clinical factors. The OPO contacts the transplant hospitals of matched patients where
doctors will determine if the donated organ is
right for their patient. Once an organ has been accepted, the clock starts ticking because organs remain
viable outside the body for only a short time. The organs are then respectfully recovered from the generous donor. The OPO arranges to
transport the donated organ to the transplant hospital, to help a patient in need. Once the medical team
transplants the organ, a life is saved. (heart beating) The donor, a willing
family, and saving organs are essential to the transplant journey. It takes place 24 hours
a day, 365 days a year. Explore how we save lives together

title: Liver Transplant - Who Can Donate It? Donors Criteria, Risks- Part 1 || Dr. Vasudevan K.R.
description:
Know all about Liver Transplant donor criteria, rules, guidelines, who can donate it, and the risks. This video features Dr. Vasudevan K.R., who leads the liver transplant and HPB surgery team at Jaypee Hospital, Noida. He has been practising liver and HPB surgery for the last 15 years. He explains two sources of liver donation which include:
Living donation: A relative can donate a portion of the liver, usually two-thirds.
Deceased donation: A patient that is brain dead and is kept alive with the help of machines in the hospital. In such a situation, the family wishes to donate many organs, including the liver.
 
Furthermore, he mentions how the law allows only a relative to donate, showcasing pure emotional attachment and love for the patient. So it is a legal requirement in India that the donor is related to the patient. However, from a medical point of view, a non-blood relative can also donate the liver, and the law accepts it if the intention behind the donation is pure love for the recipients and it happens rarely. The process to obtain approval is also very long and occurs if the patient and donor have known each other for decades and are of similar financial standing.
 
Additionally, around 40-60% of a healthy donor’s liver is removed and transplanted into the sick patient, and it is a relatively safe procedure. Moreover, the additional safety margin in liver donation, especially in living related or partial living donors, is that the liver grows back to nearly its pre-donation size and volume in 2 months.
 
In the case of a deceased donor/brain-dead donor, the quality of liver function needs to be evaluated by doing a blood test and some imaging to make sure the liver isn’t damaged during an accident, which might have caused the brain death. However, in living donation, two things are evaluated: the quality and the amount of the liver one can get and if the donor can withstand the operation. For the same, multiple blood tests, C.T. scans and MRIs are conducted to estimate the quality of the liver and its functions, and a whole body evaluation is also conducted.

description:
Transplantation of bone marrow or stem cells offers hope and a chance for a cure for many patients. For patients diagnosed with lymphoma, multiple myeloma, acute or chronic leukemia, Hodgkin's or non-Hodgkin's disease, testicular cancer,  myelodysplastic syndrome, or aplastic anemia, the Henry Ford Bone Marrow Stem Cell Transplant Program provides personalized care with patient outcomes equal to or better than the national rates.

Established in 1988, the nationally accredited Henry Ford Bone Marrow Stem Cell Transplant Program offers all three types of transplantation: autologous (patients receive their own cells), allogeneic (patients receive matching cells from a related or unrelated donor), and syngeneic (for identical twins only). We performed Michigan's first peripheral blood stem cell transplantation and regularly perform some of the most complex stem cell transplants in the country.

title: Paired Liver transplant
description:
You may have seen or heard stories about transplant chains, also known as paired donations. This is when a living donor is not a match for a specific recipient but still agrees to donate, setting off a chain reaction of transplants. Most of these paired donations involve the kidney. title: Preparing for your Transplant Surgery
description:
Sue Cutshall, R.N., C.N.S., Integrated Health Specialist and Surgical Coach in Department of Surgery, highlights important tips to prepare you for your transplant. 

• Retaining information - Bring paper or a journal to your appointments to write down instructions, thoughts, or questions that you may have for your healthcare team.  

• Caregivers - Invite your caregivers to your appointments. Consider getting together with your caregivers and discussing needs that you may have after your surgery. 

• Physical condition -- Think of ways to increase physical activities throughout the day. Be mindful of what you are putting in your body. Aim for 7-8 hours of restful sleep each night.

Amyloidosis is a disease where abnormal proteins form fibrils and deposit in organs such as the heart and kidneys.  Transthyretin is a normal protein that is made in the liver.  Those proteins are then circulated in the blood.  This is a normal process, however, if an inherited abnormality is introduced, the pathway is changed and these proteins can deposit into the organs causing people to feel unwell.  Symptoms of transthyretin amyloidosis are shortness of breath, changes in bowel habits, reduced exercise stamina, and numbness or tingling.
 
Treatment for transthyretin amyloidosis can include liver transplantation done through a donor program or through a living donor.
