I'm Dr. Andrew Bentall, a kidney doctor
at Mayo Clinic. I look after patients
with kidney disease, either in the early stages, or with more advanced
kidney disease considering dialysis and transplantation as
treatment options. In this video, we'll cover the basics of chronic
kidney disease. What is it? Who gets it? The symptoms, diagnosis
and treatment. Whether you are looking
for answers for yourself or for
someone you love, we're here to give you the best information
available. Chronic kidney disease is a disease characterized by progressive
damage and loss of function in
the kidneys. It's estimated that
chronic kidney disease affects about one in
seven American adults. And most of those don't
know they have it. Before we get into
the disease itself, let's talk a
little bit about the kidneys and
what they do. Or kidneys play many
important roles keeping our
bodies in balance. They remove waste
and toxins, excess water from
the bloodstream, which is carried out
of the body in urine. They helped to
make hormones to produce red
blood cells, and they turn
vitamin D into its active form, so it's
usable in the body. There are quite
a few things that can cause or put you at higher risk for chronic kidney disease. Some of them are not things that can
be avoided. Your risk is simply
higher if you have a family history of certain genetic
conditions like polycystic kidney
disease or some autoimmune
diseases like lupus or IgA nephropathy.
Defects in the kidney structure can also cause your
kidneys to fail, and you have an
increased risk as you get older. Sometimes, other common
medical conditions can increase your risk. Diabetes is the most common cause of
kidney disease. Both type 1 and
type 2 diabetes. But also heart disease
and obesity can contribute to the damage that causes kidneys to fail. Urinary tract issues and inflammation in
different parts of the kidney can also lead to long-term
functional decline. There are things that
are more under our control: Heavy or long-term use
of certain medications, even those that are
common over-the-counter. Smoking can also be a contributing factor to chronic kidney disease. Often there are no
outward signs in the earlier stages of chronic kidney disease, which is grouped
into stages 1 through 5 Generally, earlier stages are known as 1 to 3. And as kidney
disease progresses, you may notice the
following symptoms. Nausea and vomiting,
muscle cramps, loss of appetite, swelling via feet and ankles, dry, itchy skin,
shortness of breath, trouble sleeping,
urinating either too much or too little. However, these are usually
in the later stages, but they can also happen
in other disorders. So don't automatically
interpret this as having
kidney disease. But if you're experiencing anything that
concerns you, you should make an appointment
with your doctor. Even before any
symptoms appear, routine blood work can indicate that
you might be in the early stages of
chronic kidney disease. And the earlier
it's detected, the easier it is to treat. This is why
regular checkups with your doctor
are important. If your doctor suspects the onset of chronic
kidney disease, they may schedule a
variety of other tests. They may also refer you to a kidney specialist, a nephrologist like myself. Urine tests can reveal abnormalities
and give clues to the underlying cause of the chronic
kidney disease. And this can also help to determine the
underlying issues. Various imaging tests
like ultrasounds or CT scans can be done to help your doctor
assess the size, the structure, as well as evaluate the
visible damage, inflammation or stones
of your kidneys. And in some cases,
a kidney biopsy may be necessary. And a small amount of
tissue is taken with a needle and sent to the pathologist for
further analysis. Treatment is
determined by what is causing your kidneys to not function normally. Treating the cause is key, leading to reduced
complications and slowing progression
of kidney disease. For example, getting better blood
pressure control, improved sugar control
and diabetes, and reducing weight are often key interventions. However, existing damage is not usually reversible. In some conditions,
treatment can reverse the cause
of the disease. So seeking medical review is really important. Individual complications 
vary, but treatment might include high blood pressure
medication, diuretics to reduce
fluid and swelling, supplements to
relieve anemia, statins to lower
cholesterol, or medications to
protect your bones and prevent blood
vessel calcification. A lower-protein diet may also be
recommended. It reduces the
amount of waste your kidneys need to
filter from your blood. These can not only
slow the damage of kidney disease, but make you feel better as well. When the damage
has progressed to the point that
85 to 90 percent of your kidney function
is gone, and they no longer work well enough
to keep you alive, it's called end-stage
kidney failure. But there are still
options. There's dialysis, which uses a
machine to filter the toxins and
remove water from your body as
your kidneys are no longer able to do
this. Where possible, the preferred therapy
is a kidney transplant. While an organ
transplant can sound daunting, it's actually often the
better alternative, and the closest
thing to a cure, if you qualify for a
kidney transplant. If you have
kidney disease, there are
lifestyle choices. Namely quit smoking. Consuming alcohol
in moderation. If you're overweight
or obese, then try to lose weight. Staying active and
getting exercise can help not only with your weight, but fatigue and stress. If your conditional allows, keep up with your routine, whether that's
working, hobbies, social activities, or
other things you enjoy. It can be helpful to talk to someone you trust, a friend or relative
who's good at listening. Or your doctor could also
refer you to a therapist or
social worker. It can also be
helpful to find a support group
and connect with people going
through the same thing. Learning you have chronic kidney
disease and learning how to live with it
can be a challenge. But there are
lots of ways to help you to be more comfortable for
longer before more drastic
measures are needed. And even then, there
is plenty of hope. If you'd like to
learn even more about chronic
kidney disease, watch our other related
videos or visit Mayo Clinic.org.
We wish you well.

description:

caption_text:
>> Hi, I'm Sue Thavarajah. I'm one of the Nephrologists
at Johns Hopkins, and welcome to the ABCs
of kidney disease. In this section today, we're going to review management
of chronic kidney disease. We're going to start with talking
a little bit about medications. Now the medications are broken
down into two categories. They're either prescribed to treat the risk factors that can
speed up kidney damage, so blood pressure medications, diabetes medications are all part
of your kidney treatment plan. Then there are medications
that we prescribe to manage the complications
of kidney disease. If people develop anemia, the medications such as the iron or the erythropoietin are part
of that treatment plan. Not everyone will get
the same treatment plan. It's really going to be
individualized based on what your risk factors for kidney
disease progression are, and what other health
conditions you have, and what your lab
work is looking like. Now there's some basic
recommendations we give to people regardless of the
type of kidney disease they have and the stage
that they have in terms of some things that can
help slow down the progression. One are some of the
basic dietary changes. We want to restrict
the sodium intake to less than two grams a day. We want to reduce the consumption
of processed foods and high sugary foods because those are all things that the kidneys have
to work harder to get rid of. We talk about a moderate
protein restriction. We need a certain amount of protein
to maintain our muscle mass, maintain our immune system, but too much protein, our body can't use and our kidneys have to work harder
to get rid of it. Then there's more discussion lately about using
plant-based options. Those are sometimes better choices because they have a lower amount of uric acid and a lower
amount of cholesterol. Sometimes swapping out
some of the meals for a plant-based option will help with slowing down the
progression of kidney issues. Now there's always a lot of
discussion about water intake. You do want to stay hydrated
because dehydration can cause some changes in
your kidney function panel. But there's no specific
amount of water that someone needs to drink unless they have
a history of kidney stones. Now you may be on certain
water restrictions or fluid restrictions depending on what other health
conditions you have. This is going to be individualized and driven by discussions you
have with your health care team. Now your doctor will also give you other guidelines for your
diet based on your lab work. Some people might be on
a potassium restriction, some people might be on a
phosphorus restriction, but that's not 100 percent across the board for people
who have kidney disease. Just because you hear
about somebody else being treated with those
dietary restrictions doesn't mean that that would be what you need to have done
for your kidney disease. When we're doing those restrictions, it's really to try
to accommodate what the kidneys can't get
rid of efficiently. When we look at the overall plan for slowing down the
progression of kidney disease, it comes down to a couple of
categories: Blood pressure control, blood sugar control,
smoking cessation, regular exercise, reduction of protein in the
urine if you have that, and keeping a healthy weight. Now these are standard recommendations
regardless of what type of kidney disease you might have or what level of kidney
issues you have. When we also talk about
kidney disease progression, we also want to worry
about things that could put an extra
stressor on the kidneys, so we keep in mind things
like imaging studies that use contrast may have an
impact on the kidney function. It doesn't mean that you
don't have those studies. It doesn't mean that those
studies may not be necessary. But it is something
that you would discuss with your health care
team to see if that's an appropriate choice
for you or what they can do to help reduce your
risk of having problems. Also, medication interactions can be harmful when people
have kidney issues. No one can look at you and know what your level of kidney function is. A lot of us go to multiple different doctors or we might go to an urgent care center. It's really important
for you to be able to know what your level
of kidney function is, or makes sure that if somebody is
prescribing medications for you, that they're aware that
you have kidney disease, so they pick medications
that are going to be safe for the kidneys
or adjust the dosing. You want to be careful
with regular use of non-steroidal
anti-inflammatory agents such as ibuprofen and Motrin, Advil. Those agents are over the counter, so people often think that
they can't cause any harm. Some of these can interact with your blood pressure medications or prevent your blood
pressure from being under good control and
long-term use can end up causing some scarring and
some damage in the kidneys. You also want to be careful
with some of the bowel agents, such as milk of magnesia and some
of the preps for colonoscopy. You want to make sure
people know that you have kidney issues so that they
prescribe the appropriate one. If you're ever unsure, double-check with your pharmacist or your physician before
starting any new medications. Another key part of kidney
disease management is really being engaged and being
part of your health care team. You want to be monitoring
your progress by tracking your labs and
knowing what the trend is, you want to know your
medications and ask questions as to what they're
for and how to take them, you want to be engaged with
that health care team, and you want to incorporate
healthy lifestyle choices because that overall will
help your outcomes. Ask for help. If you're
struggling with dietary choices, if you don't know what to
do with your medications, there's teams of people
that are taking care of you that are willing to
help and they just need to know what
resources you need. Thank you for listening to
our presentation today. This was part of Johns Hopkins Nephrology Patient Education Program with the goal of improving lives of individuals living
with kidney disease. If you want to learn more, here are several
resources which have information about being engaged
in your own health care, learning what your labs mean, learning what your
different medications are, and some different dietary
choices. Thank you.

caption_text: In terms of the ability to reverse your kidney disease, it really depends on the cause of your kidney disease. Is it something transient like an infection, like a medication that you shouldn't have taken? And in those cases, you take away the insult, it is possible that you reverse your kidney disease. But it also depends on whether you had underlying kidney disease to begin with. But unfortunately for most of our population the reasons for kidney disease are longstanding such as hypertension and diabetes and unfortunately those are not reversible and therefore the kidney disease is unreversible. Unfortunately there's no cure for kidney disease but there are ways to slow down the progression of kidney disease and this is where keeping in close touch with your health care professional becomes crucial. It is important that they keep tabs on your blood tests, on the status of your health, how you feel, so that the progression does get slow down as much as possible.

and other members of the transplant team please still take the time to read your binder which has additional information not covered in this video in an effort to ensure all of your questions are answered it is recommended that you take notes along the way and touch base with your transplant coordinator for clarification or further detail on any particular topic this would be the time to pause ones and also with close outpatient follow-up at the Transplant Institute you will need to see here a transplant doctor on a weekly basis for at least the next six weeks your transplant coordinator findings on the transplant daily record shown here and bring it with you to every appointment some anti-rejection medications like prednisone can elevate blood sugars this will be discussed further in the pharmacy chapter of this video we will ask some patients to check their blood Sugar's at home also it is not uncommon to require insulin at home in these cases we will let you know what to do and you do not run out please call your pharmacy for refills at least 5 to 7 days before running out of your medications it is best to call the transplant coordinator monday through friday during business hours however if you require a refill over the weekend please contact the on-call TransLink coordinator do not wait until Monday and never wait until the last pill if you cannot take your medications for any reason please let the transplant coordinator know right away if you vomit up your medications do not take another dose unless you can see the pill in our confident it did not stay down never make changes to your meds without checking with the transplant coordinator there may be times when you wish to take in over-the-counter medication let's say for a minor ache or pain for example in hot tubs and fresh water ponds as well do not change the cat's litter box or clean pet cages please wear a mask gloves and clean your hands very thoroughly if you absolutely must it is not recommended generally not have vaccines for three months following transplant surgery and for three months treatment of rejection be careful around people who have recently had live virus vaccines be especially mark please check with your doctor about nasal flu mist as this is often a live vaccine please do not smoke smoking puts you at higher risk for infection in blood clots smoking causes long-term damage to your lungs and also increases your risk for cardiovascular disease do not drink alcohol if you have received a liver transplant as this may cause accelerated damage to your new liver after three months kidney and pancreas recipients can likely have an occasional alcoholic beverage it is best to check with your doctor before having your first drink do not eat or drink grapefruit as this fruit can interact with your anti-rejection medications and may affect how they work in your body in regards to your bowels constipation is a common side effect of pain medications if you get constipated you may try an over-the counter stool softener or a gentle laxative please refer to the over-the-counter medication guide in your binder for more detail do not take any other non prescription remedies without checking with your transplant coordinator doctor or pharmacist on the other extreme if you experience diarrhea it could be from a number of reasons diarrhea may be a side effect of some of your new transplant medications or it may be into certain infections or viruses if you have diarrhea do not take any anti diarrheal medications avoid Gatorade or any other electrolyte supplements and do your best to stay well hydrated if the diarrhea does not resolve in 24 hours please call your transplant coordinator or doctor in regards to your incision it is not uncommon to have slight redness around the stitches or staples you may also feel a firm Ridge along the incision or experience numbness around the incision all of this is normal and should improve or go away all together for your safety please use caution around heat or open flames as you may not have normal sensation and could therefore suffer a burn please contact your transplant team immediately if you develop increased redness swelling or pain around the incision or if there is any bright red or foul-smelling discharge coming from the wounds these types of symptoms are not normal and need to be addressed immediately you may shower but no bathing or swimming until your incision is completely healed you may gently wash your incision with mild soap and water pat it dry and then leave it open to the air do not use augments or powders on the incision you may have steri-strips on your incision if so they will fall off gradually they are generally removed at two weeks but it's okay if they fall off on their own before then please avoid direct sun exposure to the incision for about six to twelve months your incision will fade and become less prominent over time after the first three to six months you will gradually start seeing your transplant team less often and it will be important for you to follow up with your primary care physician in other specialists to maintain your health for regular check-ups common medical problems like the cold or flu or the management of chronic pain issues you should see your PCP it is important that you keep up to date with all recommended routine cancer screening lubrication in women in a rectal function in men may change please discuss this with us as neaten returning to work following organ transplantation this is an important goal towards getting you back title: Kidney Transplant: Deceased Donors
description: Kidney Transplant: Deceased Donors, featuring David Wojciechowski, D.O. From a seven-part video series that aims to share information on kidney transplantation at UT Southwestern.
caption_text: (soft upbeat music) Hello, my name is David Wojciechowski. I'm a transplant nephrologist and the medical director of the Kidney Transplant Program here at UT Southwestern Medical Center. Today I'm gonna spend the next few minutes speaking with you about the different types of deceased donor options that you have available as a potential transplant recipient. So as you know, when you're listed for transplant, there are many different types of deceased donors that are potentially available. They've fall into many different categories, which are listed on this slide, and we're going to go through each of these categories in a little bit more detail over the subsequent slides. The first type of deceased donor that we'll talk about is what's called an high KDPI Donor. KDPI stands for the kidney donor profile index, and it's based on the characteristics of the donor at the time of their death. Different factors go into this calculation that give the score of 0 to 100. Any score greater than 85 is considered a high KDPI donor. These kidneys are labeled high KDPI because they're expected to have a shorter graft survival compared to lower KDPI donors. For example, a high KDPI donor may have a history of high blood pressure, or the donor may have had a slightly elevated creatinine at the time of their death. Why would someone want to accept a high KDPI donor? Well, we know that somebody on dialysis has a higher risk of mortality or dying on dialysis while they're waiting for their transplant. So the data suggests that being able to get transplanted faster with a high KDPI kidney, even though may not be as good of a quality kidney as a lower KDPI, will actually increase your survival and help you live longer compared to staying on dialysis. Now, we don't offer these high KDPI kidneys to everybody. We suggest that patients who over the age of 60 who have a history of diabetes or who are over the age of 65 consider taking one of these high KDPI kidneys, as the data suggests that it will increase your survival compared to remaining on dialysis waiting for a higher quality kidney. Additionally, it's important to remember that kidneys of better quality or lower KDPI scores are actually preferentially allocated to younger patients, particularly pediatric recipients, as well as patients who have fewer comorbid medical conditions compared to patients who would be eligible for high KDPI kidney. When looking at their survival benefit, you can see on this slide that the five-year survival rate on dialysis is 25 out of 100 people. This is in comparison to those who accept a high KDPI kidney where the five-year survival rate after transplant with a high KDPI kidney is 70 out of 100 people. So again, there's a clear benefit in accepting one of these kidneys compared to remaining on dialysis and waiting for a higher quality kidney. The second type of kidney donor that we'll discuss is a donor that has risk criteria for disease transmission according to the Public Health Services, more commonly known as PHS. This is a donor who has a history of behaviors, such as IV drug use, recent incarceration, unprofessional tattoos or piercings, sexual behaviors, or unknown medical or social history at the time of their death. This is based on the donor's social history that we can obtain from the patient's family at the time of their death and not based on any obtained lab results. What are the benefits of accepting a PHS risk criteria donor? You may receive a transplant sooner, and you will often receive a higher quality organ when you receive a PHS donor. What are the potential risks? There's a risk of transmission of disease, but that is very low and usually manageable and typically falls far less than 1% in terms of the actual risk. When we think about the risk that you can accrue by accepting a PHS donor, we can look at this slide, and you can see that the risk of HIV or hepatitis C from one of these kidneys is incredibly low. It's less than .3 out of 100 people. This is a comparison to the risk of dying in a car accident, which is .9 out of 100 people. So this tells us that your risk of just driving to a normal appointment or the grocery store is actually higher than accepting one of these PHS kidneys. There are also some other considerations when we're looking at a PHS donor. We want to consider the five-year mortality risk when accepting or declining one of these offers. What we know is that 20% of patients die while waiting for their kidney transplant, and 19% were removed from the wait list while waiting, meaning that they were never transplanted, nor had the option to be transplanted. This suggests that accepting a PHS donor will shorten your waiting time and improve your survival compared to remaining on dialysis and waiting for a non-PHS donor. Additionally, it's important to remember that a PHS donor is very common. If you look nationally, about 1/3 of all deceased donor transplants fall under this category. So saying no to this category at the time of listing and not being willing to even entertain these offers will actually exclude many donors that are potentially available to you on the deceased donor waiting list. The third type of potential donor falls under the category of hepatitis B core positive or hepatitis C positive. The word hepatitis can sometimes sound scary, but we have to remember that in general, when we offered certain types of kidneys, we always do it in the context of being able to manage the risk. So let's first look at the hepatitis B core positive donor. This is a donor that has a natural history of immunity to hepatitis B and did not require a vaccination. The risk of transmission is less than 2% of acquiring hepatitis B from one of these donors, and if that were to occur, there are actually medications that effectively treat hepatitis B. Additionally, it's important to remember that many of you who are already on dialysis have been vaccinated against hepatitis B, so you actually have immunity against this virus, therefore, your risk of transmission is even far lower than the 2% that we just quoted. What about a hepatitis C positive donor? For our program, this falls under two categories. The first type are those who are hepatitis C positive in terms of their antibody, but they have no active virus in their blood, meaning they either had the infection and cleared it on their own or they had the infection and were treated effectively with antiviral therapy, or it's even possibly a false positive test at the time of the donor procurement. In this case, there's almost a 0% risk of acquiring hepatitis C from these donors, and we actually will check you for hepatitis C approximately one month after your transplant to ensure that there was no transmission of virus. The last type under this hepatitis category are the hepatitis C positive donors who not not only have antibody positive, but they also have virus positive. This means that they are actively infected with hepatitis C. This type of transplant requires an additional consent from you, the patient, noting that you have listened to and understood in more detail the issues associated with this type of deceased donor transplant. In this case, you actually will become positive for hepatitis C, both antibody and virus most likely, but we will actually treat you for hepatitis C approximately one to two weeks after your transplant. We know that we can cure hepatitis C 99 plus percent of the time. Therefore, we believe that the risk of remaining on dialysis actually outweighs the risk of receiving one of these kidneys knowing that we're able to effectively treat the hepatitis C after transplant. As you can see, the risk of acquiring hepatitis C from hepatitis C positive, not negative donor, is far less than .1% out of 100 people. The risk of dying again in a car accident is .9 out of 100 people. Again, the risk of things that we do in daily life seem to be higher than some of the risks that are acquired by accepting certain types of organ transplants from deceased donors. The fourth type of transplant that I will discuss is the A2B transplant into a blood type B recipient. So this sounds a little complicated. What does this mean? So as many of you know, when we look at transplant, we do look to match blood type in terms of the donor and the recipient. And in general, we're trying to match the blood type to you. Typically, we're not able to do an A blood type donor into a B blood type recipient. There is, however, one exception. If the blood type B recipient has low titers of antibodies against blood group A and the donor is the subtype of A2 blood group, we are actually able to do this transplant without any additional medication or preparation. This is possible because the A2 subtype of the A donor is poorly and minimally expressed on the donor kidney. Therefore, there's very little likelihood that the recipient will have a reaction to this donor. Now, we do have certain cutoffs for the antibody levels in the recipient. We do look for these antibodies in any blood group B recipient, and we monitor these on a regular basis to ensure that you are still eligible for this program. But this is another way for a patient who is blood type B who typically has the longest waiting time in our region to get transplanted a little bit quicker while they're waiting for their deceased donor transplant. The fifth type of donor that I will talk about is a donor who has passed away after cardiac death. So most organs today are from donors who die brain death, meaning that the heart is still beating at the time of the organ removal or procurement. In this case, however, the donor has undergone cardiac death and the heart has stopped. The risk that really comes with this donor has nothing to do with infections or any other issues. It's more that the kidney itself may be sleepy at the time of transplantation. We call that delayed graft function. That means the recipient may need a little bit of dialysis for a short period of time after the transplant while we wait for this kidney transplant to perk up or start working. In general, however, 99 plus percent of these kidneys work just fine and the patient comes off dialysis and has excellent function. And in fact, if you look at the long-term outcomes, there's actually no difference between a donation after cardiac death donor and what we would call a standard or brain dead donor. The last type of donor I will talk about falls under the HOPE Act. The HOPE Act is an act of Congress that was signed by the president a few years ago that actually allows us to utilize HIV positive donors in HIV positive recipients. In order to do this, any center that participates in this type of transplant has to do it under the guise of a clinical research study. At UT Southwestern, we perform our HOPE Act transplants under the guise of the HOPE in Action Clinical Trial that is sponsored by the National Institutes of Health. If you have HIV, our coordinators will inform the doctors at UT Southwestern and you may receive an additional phone call after your initial evaluation appointment to discuss the possibility of participating in the HOPE in Action Clinical Trial. If you decide to participate, you would need to sign a research consent, and this would allow us to offer you organs from deceased donors who are HIV positive. In this case, the main risk would be acquiring a form of HIV that is slightly different than your own and may require a change in your HIV medication regimen. You will also see an infectious disease specialist who is an expert in HIV in order to assess this risk and counsel you further about this possibility. These are the potential types of deceased donors that you could be offered, all of which may be able to shorten your waiting time and get you off dialysis faster. We look forward to seeing you in the future and hopefully, more importantly, seeing you sooner for plantation.

description:
Heart failure, also called congestive heart failure, has several symptoms including shortness of breath, fluid buildup (edema) and fatigue. If you have been diagnosed with heart failure, it's important for you to manage and keep track of symptoms and report any sudden changes to your healthcare team.
Learn more at heart.org/HF.

title: Mayo Clinic Q&A podcast: Less pain and faster recovery with minimally invasive heart surgery
description:
Smaller incisions, less pain and faster recovery are just a few reasons minimally invasive heart surgery can be a good option for patients with heart disease.

"I would define minimally invasive heart surgery, or robotic-assisted surgery as essentially performing a standard surgical operation through smaller incisions, without going through the breastbone," says Dr. Phillip Rowse, a Mayo Clinic cardiovascular surgeon.

Treating mitral valve disease is one example of how often robotic-assisted heart surgery is performed at Mayo Clinic. "Mayo treats about 120 cases, or more, robotically each year," Dr. Rowse says. "We have dedicated cardiologists who are in the room performing the echo tests at the time of surgery and right afterwards." 

In this Mayo Clinic Q&A podcast, Dr. Rowse discusses who's eligible for this surgery and what's involved with minimally invasive heart surgery.

Transcatheter aortic valve replacement,
or "TAVR", is a less invasive catheter-based procedure. It is revolutionizing
cardiac care and reducing the need for traditional open-heart surgeries. It's a treatment for aortic valve stenosis. That's when the aortic valve in the
heart functions poorly, usually due to calcification, reducing blood flow
throughout the body. - We don't take out the valve in the patient. We just move
the valve or the stuck leaflets out of the way without having to make a
surgical incision at all. A typical TAVR involves inserting a
guide wire into the femoral artery and threading it through the aorta, then
around the aortic arch and into the stenotic aortic valve and left
ventricle. A common TAVR procedure involves delivering a new valve with a
balloon catheter over that guide wire and into the stenotic valve. The balloon is then inflated, opening up the old valve and putting the new valve in place. The wire and catheter are then removed leaving behind a new, functioning aortic valve. Here you can see the new valve opening and closing and able to
restore normal blood flow. - The recovery for those patients, especially those
patients that are older, is much faster. Most of our patients stay overnight and
almost everyone goes home within 48 hours. Cardiologists at UC Davis Health
were the first in the Sacramento area to offer TAVR. They continue to lead the
way in providing groundbreaking treatment options to patients with heart
and vascular disease. - To have the opportunity to provide a minimally
invasive procedure for those particular patients who need it is really life
changing for many of them. Visit health.ucdavis.edu and search for TAVR, T-A-V-R, to learn more about TAVR at UC Davis. you

-Hello everyone, my name is Dr. Uttam Reddy and I'm the Medical Director here at the UC Irvine Kidney Transplant Program. I'd like to give you, today, a brief introduction into the world of kidney transplantation. First, I'd like to welcome you all to the University of California, Irvine health care system, where our motto is to discover, teach, and
heal. The kidney transplant team here at UCI consists of our Chief of Transplantation, Dr. Clarence Foster, myself - the transplant nephrologist and medical director - and Dr. Hirohito Ichii, another transplant surgeon. The history of kidney transplantation dates back to 1954, over 60 years ago, when the first successful kidney transplantation was performed between identical twins in Boston. Here at UC Irvine, we have been doing kidney transplantation since the late 1960s. We have done live kidney donor transplants since the early1970s, pancreas transplant since 2000. We are a Medicare approve transplant center, where our waiting list consists of over 600 patients. Annually, we perform about 50 transplants per year and we're looking to grow that number. So where does a kidney transplant occur on the body? Well, the thing you need to know is we
don't touch your native, natural kidneys. They stay in the body, in your back area,
and we perform a transplant surgery either on the right or left lower
abdominal areas of the body. So after transplantation, you will technically have three kidneys in place. What are the major advantages to kidney
transplantation? Well, the reason we're so excited about kidney transplantation is that there's a notable improvement in life expectancy, patients notice increased energy levels, improved mental and physical well-being, improved quality of life, they're more free in their day-to-day life as they no longer require dialysis, and there's less dietary and fluid restriction. Now there are some disadvantages to kidney transplantation, but the benefits typically outweigh the disadvantages. Some of these include multiple medications which potentially have some side effects, potential complications during any major
surgery and anesthesia, with kidney transplantation, there's risk of
rejection in infection which we monitor closely, and there's an increased risk of
cancer. Now there is an issue with kidney transplantation of late, where our wait list is growing at a significant number. In the late 1990s, there were about 45,000 patients on the waitlist. Currently, that number has crossed 100,000 and our transplantation rates have remained relatively stable
during the past 15 years. So the waitlist continues to grow Currently there are a 121,000 people waiting for a life-saving organ transplants in the United States. Of these, over 100,000 are on the kidney transplant waiting list. In 2014 in the United States, we have performed over 17,000 kidney transplants. The greater Los Angeles area is represented by the One Legacy organ procurement organization. So what type of kidney
transplants are there? Well there's two main types - a deceased donor kidney and a living donor kidney. As you can imagine, deceased donor kidney is someone who has been declared dead by either irreversible loss of all brain function
or cessation of heartbeat and respiration. A living donor is someone who is in excellent health and passes a rigorous health evaluation by the
transplant team. Deceased donor waiting times in the Orange County and Los Angeles areas average about 6 to 10 years before getting a kidney transplant. Now this is some of the highest waiting times in the entire country. For blood type O, which is the universal recipient, wait times can approach 10 years. For blood type A, the wait time is 7 to 8 years. For blood type B, the wait time is close to 8 to 10 years. For the universal recipient blood type AB, the wait time is 5 to 6 years. Regarding living donors patient outcomes are typically better for those who
receive a living donor kidney transplant as opposed to a deceased donor kidney
transplant. Less than 1% of kidney donors have endured medical complications. There is significantly less waiting time if a recipient receives a living donor so
they don't they don't have to wait many years for a deceased donor kidney
transplant. Surgery is scheduled when both the recipient and the living donor
have completed their evaluation and are accepted as candidates. The surgery is
done laparoscopically for the living donor with very small incisions. There
should be no donation-related costs for the living donor. With regards to these living donors, they're typically people between 21 years of age and 65 years of
age. They must be in good physical and mental health. They can be a friend,
relative, or even a complete stranger. It should be noted that they do not have to be compatible to you to be a living donor. We have here at UC Irvine a paired exchange program where if you have a living donor that's
not the same blood type we can enter the patient and recipient in the exchange program and find a potential living donor for that recipient. All donor information is confidential and it should be noted that it is illegal to buy or sell organs in the United States. For anyone interested in being a potential living donor, please  call 714-4566-256 for further information. now I mentioned previously about the paired kidney transplant donation. So imagine you have a brother or relative who would like to give you a kidney transplant but they have a different blood type. In another room, the same situation is
happening where a relative would like to donate to a potential recipient but they
have a different type. well we can do a paired swap where you
the donor would donate to that party's recipient and that party's donor would
donate to your recipient. And in that way, both parties would benefit from kidney transplantation. So how does UCI compare to the national averages in terms of deceased donor or living donor graft survival and patient survival
rates? Well as you can see here from this chart,
our outcomes are on par with the rest of the nation. So when can I be referred for
a kidney transplantation? Well this is in two major scenarios - either you have End Stage kidney disease and you're on dialysis, either hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis, or your kidney function has a GFR of less than 20 so you have advanced kidney disease where your glomerular filtration rate is less than 20. What would keep a patient from being a candidate for kidney transplantation? Some contraindication for kidney transplantation include severe cardiac, liver and lung disease, active systemic infections, a recent
diagnosis of cancer, severe obesity where your body mass index is greater than 40, poor functional status, and patients of an advanced age of greater than 70 are evaluated  on a case-by-case basis. If you have a history of chronic non-compliant, you may  not be considered for kidney transplantation. Any active mental illness or psycho-social instability and evidence of drugs, severe tobacco or alcohol abuse will also preclude candidacy for kidney transplantation. So in summary, compared to remaining on dialysis, patients undergoing kidney transplantation live longer, have a
better quality of life, and save on overall medical costs. Kidney transplantation is the optimal therapy for ESRD patients who can
undergo transplantation. Our goals here at UCI Kidney Transplant Program are to expand our program, to be a resource for a kidney transplant expertise in the
Orange County area, and to continue to provide exceptional care for a patient
in need of a kidney transplant and patients who've had a kidney transplant. Transplantation is a treatment option and a choice. It requires a lot of
commitment and hard work before and after the transplant. So let's work
together to make it a success. If you have any questions please feel free to
contact us at the UCI kidney transplant program our phone number is 714 456 8441 or you can visit us on our website. Thank you.

[Music starts] Pulmonary fibrosis is a term
that refers to a large group of interstitial lung diseases
that cause scarring in the lung tissue,
or interstitium. One subgroup is the one related
to autoimmune conditions. When working correctly,
the immune system defends the body from infections or
other types of damage by recognizing cells and tissues
from outside your body. However, with autoimmune problems,
the immune system is dysregulated and attacks a person’s own tissues,
causing inflammation and damage. The autoimmune diseases
that are commonly associated with lung disease can also be referred
to as “connective tissue diseases.” This is because they often affect
the parts of the body that hold us together, such as
our joints, muscles and skin. The autoimmune diseases most commonly
associated with interstitial lung disease are lupus, rheumatoid arthritis,
systemic sclerosis, dermato or poly-myositis,
and sjogren’s syndrome. Although we may associate these diseases
with specific organs, such as rheumatoid arthritis
and joint disease, they can affect other organs,
including the lungs. Some patients with autoimmune 
related interstitial lung disease first develop signs and symptoms
outside the lungs, such as in the joints or muscles. The evaluation of these signs and symptoms
leads to the autoimmune diagnosis. Other patients may present
with pulmonary symptoms first, and will likely be diagnosed
with interstitial lung disease by a pulmonologist. In patients with known autoimmune diseases,
lung disease can develop later, so a rheumatologist will be alert
to pulmonary symptoms, such as cough or shortness of breath. They may even recommend monitoring
with periodic lung function testing. A rheumatologist is a doctor
who specializes in the diagnosis and management of these autoimmune
or connective tissue diseases. In this case, your medical history,
physical exam findings and blood tests are used to make the specific diagnosis. Part of the evaluation
of interstitial lung disease involves looking for causes,
such as autoimmune disease. This means the pulmonologist might look
at some of the same blood tests that a rheumatologist might order,
or refer for evaluation by a rheumatologist if a connective
tissue disease is suspected. Some patients are given a very 
specific autoimmune diagnosis, such as “rheumatoid arthritis”
or “systemic sclerosis,” based on specific diagnostic criteria,
including symptoms, physical exam findings, blood tests and sometimes x-rays. In other patients, however,
there are autoimmune features present, but they don’t fulfill all the diagnostic criteria
for any one specific diagnosis, and there may be overlapping features. In this case, other terms such as “interstitial pneumonia
with autoimmune features” or “undifferentiated connective
tissue disease” might be used. Management should be coordinated
between the pulmonologist and the rheumatologist. Once the diagnosis of one of the connective tissue disease related
interstitial lung diseases is made, the primary management
consists of modifying or suppressing the immune system to some degree,
to try to halt the damage being done to the lungs and to reverse inflammation
when it's present. For those patients who have progressive fibrosis
as part of their disease state, their pulmonologist might consider
the use of an anti-fibrosis medication to slow disease progression. Additional research is ongoing
to determine the best approach to treat this type
of interstitial lung disease. Other important elements of treatment include pulmonary rehabilitation,
supplemental oxygen if needed, and management of pulmonary symptoms. Sometimes, if autoimmune interstitial
lung disease is progressive and not responding
to other therapies, lung transplantation
may be considered. Connective tissue disease 
related interstitial lung disease can have variable responses
to treatment. Some can stabilize or even
show improvement with therapy, while others can be
progressive over time. It’s important to follow up
with your doctor to monitor your symptoms
and lung function over time. For more information and support,
please visit pulmonaryfibrosis.org.

description:

Solid Organ Transplant's Impact on Mental Health: Explained
A GlobalCastMD production

Katherine Bedard-Thomas, PhD, and Kristin Rich, PhD:
Hi, I'm Katherine Bedard-Thomas, and I'm Kristin Rich. We’re both pediatric psychologists here at Cincinnati Children’s. Today, we’re going to talk about Pediatric Solid Organ Transplant and how it can impact coping and mental health -- before, during, and after transplant.

Here at Cincinnati Children’s, solid organ transplant includes liver, heart, lung, kidney and intestinal transplants. With transplant comes a significant amount of medical monitoring and life-long adherence requirements that are needed to prolong the health of you and your new organ. Because of this, some patients struggle with anxiety, sadness, medication adherence, or even the expectations set forth by the medical team.

At Cincinnati Children’s, we offer our transplant families a well-rounded psychosocial team of psychologists, social workers, child life specialists, pastoral care and school intervention specialists. During your pre-transplant evaluation, a psychologist will meet with you and your family to establish a relationship and learn about your unique situation. They can also help you process your experience and aid in the communication with your medical team to help clarify information.

It is important to note that your feelings, concerns, and questions may change over time and with experience. Over the course of your transplant journey there will likely be ups and downs. For example, you might experience:

Tearfulness or excessive worry. Fear about coming to the hospital or having a medical procedure. Irritability. Withdrawal from preferred activities. Poor sleep. Not wanting to be away from home or your family. Safety concerns or Concerns about your development. These are all issues we can help you with should they come up for you.

Your transplant team will be regularly checking in with you to see if you are experiencing any of these symptoms or behaviors and help determine how best to provide support. We want you to know that you can feel safe with us and we encourage you to please be open and honest with your team when discussing these issues.

If needed, the support of a psychologist is available both if you are admitted to the hospital or outside of the hospital. Additionally, if needed we can assist with locating a cognitive-behavioral or family therapist- or even medication management provider- closer to your home.

Thanks for watching. If you’d like more assistance with accessing mental health resources, please talk to your transplant coordinator, physician or social worker.

title: Ep. 14: Should organ transplant patients get the COVID vaccines?
description:
Transplant patients are at higher risk for COVID-19 and should get the vaccine, but only those using mRNA, says Lewis Teperman, MD, director of transplant services for Northwell Health and vice chair of surgery at North Shore University Hospital. Since the novel virus hit New York, Dr. Teperman has led the American Society of Transplant Surgeons (ASTS) strikeforce and helped write the blueprint on how to perform transplants safely during the pandemic.

Listen to the full audio podcast: https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/20-minute-health-talk/id1528414053?i=1000507430159

Chapters

00:01 - Prioritizing transplant patients for the vaccines
01:46 - Which vaccines are safe for transplant recipients?
03:37 - Testing organs and donors for COVID-19
05:10 - Becoming an organ donor during a pandemic

Prioritizing transplant patients

Transplant patients are dying from COVID-19 at a higher rate than most patients. In New York, there are more than 1,600 transplant recipients - kidneys, livers, hearts and others - all over the state that have already contracted the novel virus. Among that group there is a high overall mortality rate, which is even worse in those admitted to an intensive care unit. Unfortunately, because these patients require immunosuppressive medications to prevent their body from rejecting their new organ, they are more susceptible to severe infection.

A transplant recipient who contracts COVID-19 likely will be asymptomatic for a longer period of time, setting up a dangerous scenario where they become a super spreader. Therefore, it is critical that transplant patients receive the COVID vaccine, as recommended by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

At Northwell Health, we're working with New York State to prioritize this population, both recipients, those on waiting lists and donors. This is a comorbidity in its own right, and if they don't get vaccinated these patients are left extremely vulnerable to this virus.

Which vaccines are safe?

Both the Pfizer and Moderna vaccines work off of mRNA technology. When injected into the body, it sends a message instructing your cells to produce a spike protein that is very distinctive to COVID-19. Should you contract COVID-19, your body will now recognize this protein as a foreign body and then build an immune response to kill it — antibodies that have actual memory to combat the illness.

We recommend MRNA because there is no viral vector, meaning it does not inject the live virus that causes COVID-19. We don't believe that it will activate the immune system to cause an organ rejection, and we know that these vaccines showed greater than 90-percent efficacy in preventing infections with minimal side effects during rigorous clinical trials. We expect the same in the transplant recipients.

Some people may ask, “should the recent transplant recipient get it?” Because you are on a lot of immunosuppressive agents you may not make as robust a response to the vaccine. That may be true. It may not be true. But you won't know until you take it. Therefore, my answer is the same - if offered a vaccine take it.

Testing deceased donors and live donors

The donor pool is repeatedly tested for COVID-19. Donors are tested as many as three times. In some cases, CAT scans of the chest are also used to make sure there is no sign of any COVID. When there is even slight suspicion of active COVID, they are declined as an organ donor. There has been no transmission of a positive organ donor giving to a recipient of deceased donation. So the donor pool is incredibly safe.

Donors who have recovered from COVID-19 infection and now test negative on PCR - and perhaps even test positive for antibodies - we allow to donate. Because they have cleared the virus they may actually convey some antibodies to the recipient.

Living donors should have a higher priority for the vaccine, too. These individuals are healthcare workers, because they allow patients to come off of dialysis, prevent liver failure, heart failure and death.

Becoming an organ donor

Living donation plummeted in the New York area at the height of the pandemic in early 2020. High rates of COVID in an area make transplant surgery very dangerous. But, now that numbers of cases are going down in New York and surgeries have resumed, we need to increase the donor pool. While the DMV remains closed, anyone can and should sign up online with your local DMV.

caption_text:
Hello, on behalf of the Froedtert & the 
Medical College of Wisconsin Kidney and   Pancreas Transplant Program, I would like to 
welcome you to our video education series on   transplant. During this video, we will cover 
the role of the transplant financial liaison. A   transplant financial liaison is a professional 
who helps with financial matters and hospital   billing related to a transplant. They will 
work with other members of the transplant team,   insurance companies and administrative 
personnel to coordinate the financial   aspects of all care related to transplant. 
They will help determine how patients can best   pay for their transplant. It is important for 
patients to have sufficient insurance benefits   to be eligible for transplant. It is our job to 
make sure that patients have proper coverage,   and they understand what is required of them 
before and after receiving a transplant. A   transplant financial liaison will meet with 
patients in the Transplant Clinic during the   transplant evaluation. There are a few things 
patients should be ready to discuss. First, the   liaison will review current and past employment, 
as well as current income. This will let us know   if there are any short- or long-term disability 
benefits available through the employer.   We also need to know if patients are receiving 
Social Security benefits or a pension. This   will help the transplant team understand if there 
are additional coverage options available. Next,   the liaison will review the current insurance plan 
or plans a patient has. There will be a discussion   around what benefits are offered and how much 
a patient may be expected to pay, as well as   if there are any limitations on where services can 
be provided. The liaison will then talk about the   three parts of Medicare, as well as the different 
ways patients can become eligible for Medicare.   The liaison will determine at the clinic visit 
if a patient is eligible for Medicare or when   they may become eligible in the future. Another 
topic that will be covered briefly is living   donation and how those services are covered. 
Patients will receive a list of the medications   commonly taken after transplant. The list 
will include how these medications are billed,   including what the patient out-of-pocket costs 
will be for each one. Additionally, options   will be shared to help lower out-of-pocket costs. 
Finally, the liaison will determine if a patient   needs any additional help, including fundraising 
options that are available to transplant patients.   As a member of the transplant multidisciplinary 
team, the financial liaison is there before and   after transplant to help patients navigate the 
costs associated with their transplant. You have   reached the end of this video. We encourage you 
to continue watching the videos in this series   on kidney transplant. Thank you for choosing

title: CF Foundation | COVID-19 Vaccine Update: Transplant Recipients
description:
This week, the Journal of the American Medical Association published the first data of its kind around COVID-19 vaccination among transplant recipients. The study, which was authored by researchers at @JohnsHopkins, found that people who are post-transplant are shown to have a much lower immune response to the vaccine.

Al Faro, the vice president of clinical affairs at the CF Foundation, discusses with Sarah Alspach, chief communications officer at the CF Foundation, what this update means for members of the cystic fibrosis community who have received a transplant.

0:00 | COVID-19 Vaccine Update: Transplant Recipients
0:26 | What does the Johns Hopkins University study mean for people who have received a transplant, including lung transplant recipients with cystic fibrosis?
2:12 | What do we know about the study participants, and were there any differences in how they responded to the COVID-19 vaccines?
3:16 | What does this mean for people with cystic fibrosis who have received a transplant, like a double lung transplant? Should they follow the recent CDC guidance about what fully vaccinated people can do?
5:36 | The study looked at participants after they had received the first dose of the vaccine. Do the researchers from John Hopkins University plan to do a follow-up, once post-transplant recipients have received the second dose of the COVID-19 vaccine?
6:11 | How can other immunocompromised groups participate in research about COVID-19 vaccines?
6:48 | Should people who are post-transplant still get vaccinated?

Originally recorded March 17, 2021

May 5, 2021: A new study published in the Journal of American Medical Association (JAMA) suggests that a large percentage of transplant recipients remain at risk for COVID-19, even after two doses of mRNA (Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna) COVID-19 vaccines. You can read about the results of the study here: https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2779852

Learn more about the national vaccine research study for transplant recipients: https://transplantvaccine.org/

Hello, this is Sarah Alspach, chief communications 
officer at the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation I'm joined today by Dr. Al Faro,
vice president of clinical affairs and lead of the lung transplant

of its kind around COVID-19 vaccination  among solid organ transplant recipients – 
including lung transplant patients –  was published in the Journal of 
American Medical Association.  The study, which was authored by 
researchers at Johns Hopkins University  found that that people 
who are post-transplant are shown to have a much lower immune 
response to the vaccine than others. More specifically, the study included 436 
people who were post-transplant  and had not previously been
infected by COVID-19. Among those patients – only 17% 
had detectable antibodies. Now, if you remember, antibodies are the proteins 
that are produced by the immune system  to fight off an infection. So, only 17% had antibodies to COVID-19, 
after receiving the first dose of either the  Pfizer-BioNTech or Moderna 
COVID-19 vaccine.  This is a stark contrast to the general 
population, where 100% of people were shown to have 
some detectable antibodies after receiving their first 
dose of either vaccine. Importantly, these data indicate that 
people who are post-transplant  and have received the vaccine may 
not be as protected as others,  remain at higher risk for COVID-19, 
despite vaccination  and need to continue taking precautions. Thanks, Al.  This is certainly important information 
for the transplant community. Is there any more information 
about the patients in this study and differences in how they 
responded to the vaccine? The findings from the study were not 
consistent across all patient groups. Those who are on certain types 
of immunosuppressive medications  called antimetabolites such as 
mycophenolate (Cellcept) or azathioprine (Imuran), were about five times less likely 
to develop antibody responses –  which indicates the level 
of protection in your body. Older recipients, over 40 and especially 
over 60 were less likely to develop an antibody response. When you look at organs specifically, lungs 
were the least likely to mount a response – most likely due to the immunosuppression 
they are typically on. So, what does this mean for 
the CF lung transplant community?  Should they follow the recent CDC guidance 
about what fully vaccinated people can do, and I am thinking particularly about 
the guidance around visiting with  unvaccinated individuals from single households 
who may not be at high risk for COVID-19? Sarah, it pains me to say this, 
but the answer is no.  In fact, the CDC did issue guidance that 
“people should discuss with their provider  if they have questions about their individual situation,
such as immunocompromising conditions” but it is buried in the guidance text 
and has not received media attention. Given the outcomes of this study and the known 
fact that transplant recipients immune systems  may not produce as strong a response to the 
vaccine because of their transplant medications, the lung transplant community 
must remain vigilant and  continue to take the necessary 
precautions to stay safe and healthy. It is important to note that patients should 
not on their own stop or reduce their immunosuppression in the hopes that it 
might improve their response to the vaccine. Stopping or reducing the doses of these 
medications can have serious consequences and might result in rejection. Transplant recipients should discuss 
their concerns with their transplant team. People who have had a transplant should 
continue to take precautions against infection, including physical distancing, washing hands 
frequently, and wearing a face covering as should the people who 
live in the same household. We also strongly encourage that family 
members in households of transplant patients receive the vaccine when 
they are able to get one. Vaccinating those around a person who is immune 
suppressed could help protect them from the virus. Thanks, Al. Now, the study looked at patients
after they received the first dose of the vaccine. Do the researchers from Johns Hopkins plan to do 
a follow up once patients have received their second dose? This study is ongoing, and the authors indicated 
they will have data from the second dose, as well as deeper studies of 
T-cell and B-cell responses, which can indicate that a person 
has some level of immunity,  even when antibodies are not detectable. The researchers are also studying 
other immunocompromised groups. Enrollment is open now and 
they welcome new participants.  They also hope to share 
more information soon. You can learn more by 
going to: transplantvaccine.org.  I also want to add that we are aware
of other investigators who are also doing research in 
this area as well. Thanks, Al. Is there anything further you want to add?  Should people who are 
post-transplant still get vaccinated?  Sarah, I recognize that this certainly 
is not the kind of news anyone within our  CF transplant community wants to hear, 
but we wanted to ensure the community became aware of this critically important 
information as quickly as possible. Studies like this are just the start of 
the continued journey as we learn more  about the impact of COVID-19 
and lung transplant recipients. I do want our transplant community to know 
that any protection against COVID-19 is helpful,  and recommend vaccination, 
but it is important to understand that  there are limitations to the 
protection the vaccines can provide  for post-transplant patients. I encourage patients to speak directly 
with their CF and transplant teams to discuss the benefits 
and risks around vaccination. If I can offer just a slight ray of hope, 
I would say to please try and keep the faith. We are watching this very closely and
will keep you updated as soon as we learn more. There is a lot we still don’t know such as what 
the response might be after a second dose nor what future studies might show. For an example, it would not be far-fetched to 
consider studying if transplant patients might benefit from additional boosters. or studying what the clinical effectiveness of
the vaccine is in preventing serious disease in the population of the 
immunocompromised individuals. In the meantime, the CF Foundation is here 
to help support you in any way we can.  I also encourage you to reach out to 
your CF care and transplant teams  to talk through this data and guide you 
as vaccination roll-out continues. Thank you so much, Al and thank you to the 
community members who have tuned in. As Dr. Faro mentioned, there is still much to learn 
about transplantation and COVID-19 vaccines. While we might not have the all answers,

(upbeat music) - Hi. I'm Jason Denny. I'm the director of the
Center for Living Donation. I'm also the surgical director of the Living Donor
Kidney Transplant Program at Henry Ford Health. When you're called in
for a kidney transplant, you will go to the H6 floor
and be tested for COVID-19. If the COVID-19 testing is negative, you will proceed to the preoperative area, where you will meet your
surgeon and anesthesia teams. There, you'll complete your
pre-transplant testing. If you need dialysis, that can
be done prior to transplant. The surgical team will
check the transplant kidney in the operating room. If it looks okay and you look
okay, you will proceed to the operating room for four to six hours. You'll be given general anesthesia. The typical kidney transplant incision is near the right lower abdomen. During the operation, your
native kidneys are not removed. A third or fourth kidney will be placed in the
front of the stomach, usually on the right side. The native kidneys will
continue to atrophy or shrink and get smaller over time. The surgeon will create an incision and find the blood vessels that run to and from your
leg, as well as the bladder. The surgeon will implant the kidney. The kidney transplant can also be done with the assistance of a robot, which results in smaller wounds and reduced wound complications. There are three main connections made during the transplant of the kidney. The first and second surgical connections are between the transplant
renal vein and artery and the iliac vein and artery. This returns blood flow
to the transplant kidney. The ureter is a tube that carries
the urine from the kidney. A third surgical connection is made between the transplant
ureter and your bladder to drain any urine that
the kidney produces. A drain is placed near the kidney to drain any fluids that
collect around the kidney. We will be watching the amount and character of the drainage. We can remove the drain once
we are happy with the quality and the amount is less than
100 milliliters in 24 hours. A stitch is placed over the drain site at the time of removal to prevent the drain site from leaking after the drain is removed. Sometimes, it is necessary to
send you home with your drain. In this case, you will be
taught how to care for the drain and empty and record its output at home. If you are sent home with the drain, you will need to keep
the site clean and dry. Often, a stent is inserted between the ureter and the bladder. This stays for about three weeks while the surgical connection between the ureter and the bladder heals. A drain is left inside at the time of the surgery
near this connection. The drain can help remove any excess fluid from the area around the
new kidney transplant. Output from the drain
can also help identify if there is a leak, a complication where the urine is leaking
through the connection. This occurs in approximately
1 to 3% of patients. The stent is removed by
cystoscopy, an outpatient procedure which does not require general anesthesia. (upbeat music)

caption_text:
>> Rejection is the normal response of the body's immune system,
to protect you from infection. Rejection is basically inflammation. It happens when your body recognizes your new
organ as foreign, and tries to destroy it. It can be scary to hear that you have rejection. However, it is important to remember that almost
everyone will encounter this complication. In spite of all precautions, an acute
rejection episode is very common in the first year after transplant. Keep in mind that your immune system
is just trying to protect you. When this happens, your transplanted
organ becomes puffy with fluid, and some of the tissue can be injured. You may experience some shortness of
breath, or not have any symptoms at all. If the injury becomes too great, your
transplanted organ won't work properly. Most episodes of acute rejection
can be successful reversed with early detection and special medications. Some things that can lead to the development
of rejection include previous episodes of rejection, patient non-compliance
with medications -- not taking correctly or not
taking at all, and infection. Signs and symptoms of rejection are
similar to signs of an infection. They include increased shortness of
breath, cough, fatigue or tiredness, fever of 100.5 degrees Fahrenheit
or higher, chills, muscle aches, flu-like symptoms, not feeling right. Keep in mind that while you may
have one or more of these symptoms, often people do not experience
any symptoms whatsoever. This does not mean that your
rejection is any less severe. All rejections should be taken seriously. Notify your transplant coordinator
immediately if you have any of these symptoms. Now that you are immunosuppressed, it is vital that you pay close attention
to your body when you go home. You should contact your transplant coordinator
if you note any of the following signs of infection -- increased redness,
drainage, or tenderness of your incisions, a temperature exceeding 100 degree Fahrenheit by
mouth, or a persistent low-grade temperature 99 to 100 degrees Fahrenheit for more than three
days, a new cough lasting more than two days, increasing shortness of breath,
or burning when you urinate, or feeling the need to urinate frequently. There are several different causes of infection
-- bacterial, viral, fungal, and parasitic. All of these are very dangerous,
and should be avoided. There are specific drugs to
treat each type of infection. You will learn more about these
in your lung transplant class. You should check with your post-transplant
coordinator before receiving any vaccinations or immunizations. Vaccines made with live viruses pose a risk,
because the viruses can be transmitted to you. Before you have any dental work done,
or any type of medical procedure, where a device is inserted into your
mouth, throat, lungs, esophagus, or genital urinary tract, you should be
taking antibiotics to prevent infection. There are things all around you
that can make you very sick. You must take proper precautions
to guard against infection. Proper hand washing, avoiding improperly cooked
or stored food, avoiding cat litter boxes, wearing a mask and gloves when gardening can
also help minimize your risk of infection. [ Silence ]

caption_text: Welcome to our liver transplant education program. These videos will walk you through the journey of liver transplantation, covering the evaluation process, the weightless phase, the transplant operation, the hospital recovery, and what to expect after your transplant. Our goal is to help you feel informed and prepared at every step of this lifesaving process. Your liver transplant journey begins with an evaluation. This step ensures that a liver transplant is the right option for you. The evaluation includes blood tests, imaging studies, a heart evaluation, and consultations with specialists. These help us assess your liver function, overall health, and whether you're a good candidate for the procedure. In addition to physical health, we'll assess your emotional well-being and your support system. A strong support network is key to recovery. Our team will provide guidance on lifestyle changes such as diet, exercise, and managing your medications. Once you're approved for a liver transplant, you'll be placed on a national weight list. This list matches donors with recipients based on factors like blood type, body size, and medical urgency. The weight could be unpredictable as it depends on the availability of donor organs. While you wait, your condition will be monitored regularly through blood tests and checkups. Your position on the list may change over time based on your MELD score, a score that reflects how urgently you need a transplant. It's important to stay as healthy as possible during this period by following your care team's instructions closely. After surgery, you will stay in the surgical intensive care unit for close monitoring and transition to the transplant floor when you are medically stable. The average hospitalization is 7 to 10 days. During this time, you'll receive medications to prevent your body from rejecting a new liver. You will be on these medications for life. After leaving the hospital, recovery continues at home. You will need regular follow-up visits and blood tests to ensure your new liver is functioning well. Your care team will adjust your medications, which will include imunosuppressants to prevent rejection, and other drugs to support your health. The following videos will go into more detail about the evaluation phase, weight list phase, the transplant, surgery, your hospitalization, the new medications you'll be taking, and your recovery. description:
Sandip Kapur, M.D., the Chief of Transplant Surgery and Director of Kidney and Pancreas Transplant Programs at NewYork-Presbyterian/Weill Cornell Medical Center in New York City, discusses living donor kidney transplants. Specifically, this video focuses on "kidney chains" - a kind of kidney swap usually involving three or more transplants. In the arrangement, people donate kidneys to strangers so that someone they know gets a kidney in return.



You can learn more about Dr. Kapur at:

https://www.nyp.org/physician/sandipkapur

A pediatric kidney transplant has many steps and it’s helpful to know what to expect throughout the process. Watch this video to learn what happens in the hospital during and immediately after a kidney transplant.
Your child’s pediatric kidney post-transplant care focuses on monitoring and observation to make sure your child’s vital signs stay at a safe level and their recovery is going well. During in-hospital care, after your child’s transplant, doctors and nurses monitor and regulate things like blood pressure and urine with the use of tubes and catheters. Watch the video to learn how your child’s doctors and nurses keep your child safe during and after their kidney transplant.

caption_text:
In this video, we’ll be going over what
to expect during and immediately after a kidney transplant surgery at Children’s Hospital
Colorado. A kidney transplant is a very complicated
surgery, which tends to involve several tubes, drains, and overall monitoring. Before the surgery begins, your child will
be given general anesthesia, so they will not feel any pain during the procedure. While your child is asleep, the anesthesia
team may place a central line or arterial line before the kidney transplant starts. These lines help monitor blood pressure and
overall fluid status. A foley catheter will also be placed before
the operation begins. This catheter helps monitor the urine being
made by the new kidney and also helps to protect the sutures attaching the ureter to the bladder. The soonest the Foley catheter will be removed
post-transplant is 3 days. At the end of the kidney transplant, the surgical
team may choose to place a JP drain near the kidney to monitor for bleeding or urine leaking. JP drains are closed-suction devices which
collect bodily fluids from surgical sites. After the kidney transplant is done, your
child will be taken to the pediatric intensive care unit or PICU. Here the nurses will send frequent labs and
monitor your child. The surgeons will remain in constant communication
with the PICU team. An ultrasound will be done of the new kidney
when your child arrives in the PICU. The urine output will also be monitored every
hour. Your child will receive a lot of intravenous
fluid in the first 24 hours to keep the new kidney happy. This means your child may look puffy, which
is normal. There are occasions where your child may need
to be on a ventilator after the transplant or may need hemodialysis. These are both temporary measures and will
be stopped as soon as possible. Your child will be allowed to drink after
the surgery and will usually be given food the next day. For more information about kidney transplants,
please watch our video, Pediatric Kidney Transplant: Overview & Procedure.

Mycophenolate Mofetil (Cellcept) is prescribed to help prevent rejection of a transplanted organ after surgery.

title: Heart Transplant at UC Health: Your Journey Begins Here
description:
Welcome to the Advanced Heart Failure Program at UC Health. This video introduces you to the heart transplant process.    

Learn about the collaborative evaluation process between the medical team and the patient, emphasizing the need for a committed caregiver.    

Understand the barriers to heart transplantation, including active infections, substance use, and uncontrolled medical conditions.    

Get insights into the evaluation timeline and the importance of regular participation.    

This video sets the stage for your heart transplant journey, providing essential information about the initial steps.
caption_text: Welcome to the advanced heart failure program at UC Health. Today we're going to talk about the process of heart transplantation. If you're watching this video, your treatment team has recommended that you consider heart transplant. This is a big step and we'll be with you the whole way. There's a lot to learn. Evaluation for heart transplantation is an interactive process where we learn about you and you learn about us. Together we make a decision about whether heart transplantation is right for you. You cannot face heart transplant alone. It requires a committed caregiver. This person will need to undergo evaluation and education process with you. Our goal is to understand what your risk of heart transplantation is. And this is a head-to-ee evaluation that includes blood tests, diagnostic studies, and consultations. We will be evaluating your medical history, considering any prior surgery, and any medical problems that you have. There are some important barriers to heart transplant that you need to know about. Heart transplantation is not safe if you have an active infection or an active cancer. We cannot offer a heart transplant if you're an active tobacco or marijuana smoker or use any recreational drugs. Drinking alcohol in excess is a problem. If you are a former smoker or drug user, we will need 6 months of documented abstinence from use. Obesity can be a barrier to heart transplant. The body mass index or BMI is calculated and needs to be less than 35 which is a healthy BMI for surgery. Diabetes can be a barrier to transplant. It needs to be well controlled with a hemoglobin A1C less than 7.5. Your history of success taking medications is an important predictor if you will survive after a heart transplant. In fact, if you don't take your medicines regularly, take them incorrectly, or miss clinic visits, you will not be offered a heart transplant. Caregiver support, reliable transportation, and adequate insurance coverage are all essentials for heart transplant. Now, this evaluation process takes from about 1 to 3 months in total. Sometimes this evaluation takes place in the hospital, but more commonly is done in a series of coordinated outpatient visits. The process takes place at Cincinnati at UC Medical Center.
